articles.title: Stop Shipping Custom UI That Disappears in `forced-colors` Mode
articles.description: Windows High Contrast Mode doesn't just boost contrast — it strips your backgrounds, shadows, and colors outright. Here's what `forced-colors` actually does, why a styled <div> vanishes while a real <button> survives, and the fix.
articles.body_html:
A QA ticket landed with a screenshot: "Submit button missing on checkout." I opened the page in Chrome. The button was right there — blue, rounded, impossible to miss. I opened it in Firefox. Same button. I assumed a bad screenshot and closed the ticket.

Three days later it came back, same screenshot, same page, from a different tester. This time I asked what they'd changed. "Nothing," they said. "I just use Windows with High Contrast on, because I'm light-sensitive." I flipped that setting on my own machine for the first time in years, reloaded the page, and watched my button disappear into the background like it had never existed.

It wasn't a rendering bug. It wasn't a z-index fight. It was a CSS feature I'd never once had to think about, quietly rewriting my entire color palette out from under me.

The fix that didn't fix anything

My first guess was contrast. The button used background: #2563eb on a white card — readable, passed every automated contrast checker I ran. So I assumed High Contrast Mode was some kind of amplifier: it probably just needed more contrast to work with. I darkened the blue, added a heavier box-shadow for depth, bumped the border a shade, and shipped it.

The next build, the button was still gone.

That's the part that should have told me something was off: I hadn't made the colors fail a contrast check, I'd made them more correct by every metric I knew how to check — and the bug didn't budge. If contrast were the problem, a darker blue should have helped. It changed nothing, because the browser was never reading my blue in the first place.

What forced-colors actually does

Windows High Contrast Mode doesn't ask the browser to render your page with better contrast. It tells the browser to render your page using the operating system's own fixed palette — full stop, author CSS or not. Every modern browser exposes this as a media feature:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* the user has an OS-level forced-colors palette turned on */
}

It only ever matches when the user has flipped an OS-level switch (Windows High Contrast themes are the classic trigger) — you can't turn it on with JavaScript, and prefers-contrast is a different, much gentler feature that just reports a preference for more or less contrast without touching your styles at all. forced-colors is not a hint. When it's active, the browser overrides nearly every color-related property you wrote — color, background-color, border-color, outline-color — and remaps each one onto one of a couple dozen system colors, chosen by what kind of element it's on. Normal text becomes CanvasText on a Canvas background. A button's label becomes ButtonText. None of that is something your stylesheet gets a vote on.

Two more things get treated even more bluntly: box-shadow and text-shadow are forced to none, and any background-image that isn't a url() is forced to none too. There's no sensible way to remap a drop shadow or a gradient onto a small fixed palette, so the browser doesn't try — it just removes them.

Here's the part that explains my exact bug. My button's shape came from background: #2563eb plus a box-shadow for depth, and it had border: none. Under forced colors: the background got remapped to some flat system color, the shadow vanished outright, and because I'd never declared an actual border, there was nothing left for the browser to recolor into a visible edge. The button didn't get uglier — it got structurally invisible, blending straight into the page.

Quick gut check before you keep reading: if a native <button> has the exact same styles — background, box-shadow, border: none — why does it usually survive forced colors when a <div> styled to look like a button doesn't?

Why the real button survived and the fake one didn't

The difference isn't that <button> is magic. It's that most "reset" button styles only remove the parts they're actively replacing, and browsers ship a default border on form controls in their user-agent stylesheet. Unless you've specifically zeroed that out, there's still a border on a native <button> for forced colors to recolor into something visible. A <div> built from scratch as a custom checkbox or button usually never had a border at all — its shape existed only in the properties forced colors throws away.

This is a known enough pattern that there's a standing trick for it: give decorative edges a border: 1px solid transparent instead of border: none in your normal styles. Visually, nothing changes — a transparent border is invisible either way. But forced colors mode remaps border colors, including transparent, onto the system palette. You get a free, correctly colored boundary in forced-colors mode without touching how the component looks the other 99% of the time anyone views it.

The actual fix

The reliable fix isn't fighting the override — it's meeting it, explicitly, with the same palette the browser is already using. System color keywords like ButtonBorder, ButtonFace, Highlight, and CanvasText are valid CSS values any time, and forced colors mode treats them as already correct, so it leaves them alone instead of remapping them to something else:

.custom-checkbox {
  background: #2563eb;
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 2px #93c5fd;
  border: none;
}

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .custom-checkbox {
    /* box-shadow is gone here no matter what — give it a real border instead */
    border: 1px solid ButtonBorder;
    background: ButtonFace;
  }

  .custom-checkbox[aria-checked="true"] {
    background: Highlight;
    border-color: Highlight;
  }
}

Nothing in the normal-mode styles changes. Inside the media query, the checkbox gets an explicit border using a keyword that already means "the border color controls should have," and its checked state uses Highlight, the same system color the browser uses for selected text and active UI. The result matches how every native control on that user's machine already looks — which is the entire point of the feature.

There's one more lever worth knowing, and it's a trap if you reach for it too fast: forced-color-adjust: none opts an element out of all of this, so your original colors render exactly as written, forced colors mode or not — in browsers that support the property. Unlike forced-colors itself, forced-color-adjust isn't Baseline yet: Chrome and Firefox support it, but Safari doesn't, as of this writing — so don't treat it as a guaranteed universal escape hatch, and still test the element without it. It's tempting to slap it on the whole page the moment you see something break. Don't. The moment you opt out, you own the contrast and visibility guarantees the user just told their OS they need — that's appropriate for a brand logo or a purely decorative illustration, and actively harmful on real text or an interactive control. If you ever use it, use it narrowly, and never on anything the user has to read or click.

Test it before a bug report does

The quickest way to see all of this without touching a single Windows setting: Chromium-based DevTools (Chrome, Edge) can emulate forced colors mode directly — open the Rendering tab and look for the CSS media feature emulation options, flip forced-colors to "active," and reload. Every property swap in this post happens live, on your own page, in your own browser.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

What I actually changed

I didn't rewrite the design system. I added one @media (forced-colors: active) block per component that relied on shadows or background color for its shape, each one just a border and maybe a background swap using system keywords. The checkout button that started this whole thing now has four extra lines of CSS. It's visible to every High Contrast user it was invisible to before, and it looks exactly the same to everyone else.

The lesson that actually stuck with me isn't about this one bug. It's that "I tested it and it looks fine" has a hidden asterisk: fine in whose color scheme. Dark mode earned a place in every component checklist a few years ago. Forced colors deserves the same five-second check before you call something done — because the first time you hear about it, like me, it'll be from someone who can't see your product at all.

articles.description: RelationCanvas is a relationship chart editor for fiction writers: characters are cards,...
articles.body_html:
RelationCanvas is a relationship chart editor for fiction writers: characters are cards, relationships are labeled arrows. It has no accounts and no database. The server sends the pages and the JavaScript, and it never receives a chart. That decision shaped three parts of the code: saving, PNG export and sharing. Here's how each one works. (It's a Next.js 16 and React 19 app, but none of this depends on the framework.)

One format for everything

A chart is a JSON object wrapped in a small envelope: a format name (relationcanvas), a version number (1) and the chart itself. The chart holds a title, a credit line, a legend toggle, the people (id, name, position, optional picture, note and colour) and the relationships (from, to, and a label that is either a preset or custom text).

The same envelope is used for browser storage, for the downloadable project file, and inside share links. One parser reads all three, so a file can't be accepted in one place and rejected in another. Share links get an extra, stricter key check on top.

Saving to localStorage

Every change is written to localStorage under one key, relationcanvas.chart.v1, with a revision number added to the stored JSON. That sounds like one line of code. The edge cases took most of the work.

Data that won't parse. If the stored value fails validation, the editor copies the raw string to a second key (relationcanvas.chart.v1.backup), starts with an empty chart and shows a notice saying the old data was kept aside. If that backup can't be confirmed, saving is blocked rather than risk overwriting the only copy.

Two tabs. Before each write, the editor reads the stored revision. If it differs from the revision this tab loaded, the write is treated as a conflict, not an overwrite. The editor also listens for the browser's storage event, so when another tab saves, this tab can adopt the newer chart if it has no unsaved changes of its own.

Storage that fails. When a write fails, the editor retries with a delay that starts at one second and doubles up to a 30-second cap. If storage can't be read at all, the notice tells the user to download a project file to keep new work.

Pictures. A character picture is cropped to a square in the browser and stored as a data URL inside the chart. The encoder tries PNG at 256, 192 and 128 pixels, then WebP at quality 0.9, 0.75 and 0.6, and keeps the first result under 120,000 characters. The cap puts a known ceiling on what one picture adds to storage.

The honest limit: clearing site data deletes the chart. The site says so, and the File menu has Download project file and Import project for backups and moving devices.

PNG export without a server

The chart is drawn by a function that returns an SVG string. The same renderer produces the export preview and the read-only share view.

Export takes that SVG, serializes it into a Blob with type image/svg+xml, loads it through an object URL into an image element, and draws the image onto a canvas that has been filled with the theme's background colour. canvas.toBlob produces the PNG, which downloads as relationcanvas.png.

Three details came from things going wrong:

  • Scale. The user picks 2x or 4x. The dialog shows the final pixel size and the line "Full chart · No watermark" before downloading.
  • Size limits. If either side would exceed 16,384 pixels, or the total would pass 32,000,000 pixels, export refuses and suggests 2x or moving the characters closer together.
  • A blank-image check. After drawing, the code reads the top-left pixel. If it doesn't match the background colour, the export reports a failure instead of handing over an empty file.

Sharing without a database

A share link is a URL to /view with the chart in the fragment, after the #. The fragment has three dot-separated parts: a version tag (rc1), the project JSON compressed with the browser's CompressionStream in deflate-raw mode and encoded as base64url, and a base64url SHA-256 digest of the compressed bytes.

Browsers don't send the fragment to the server, so names and labels stay out of request logs.

Two rules keep links usable:

  • No pictures. Avatars are removed before encoding. The share dialog says "Images aren't included in this link. PNG export keeps them."
  • 2,000 characters, total. The whole URL, not only the fragment, has to fit in 2,000 characters, because a normal Discord message is 2,000 characters and a longer one turns into a text file instead of a link. If the chart is too big, there's no link, and the editor suggests Export PNG and a project file.

The viewer is defensive about what it accepts. It checks the digest before decompressing. It caps decompression at 4,968,766 bytes, which is twice the size of the largest chart the editor can produce (20 people, every field at its limit, 2,484,383 bytes). It then checks the JSON against a fixed list of allowed keys before turning it into a chart. Older links without the digest still open, because a link someone has already posted should keep working.

The /view page is noindex, follow, so shared charts don't end up in search results.

What this design gives up

A chart lives in one browser profile. There's no sync between devices beyond the project file. Share links are read-only snapshots, not collaboration. Large charts can't be shared as links at all. The editor is designed around casts of up to 20 people, and the limits above are sized for that.

If you've built something similar with localStorage, I'd like to know how you handled two tabs editing the same data.

I drafted this article with help from an AI assistant. The technical details come from the project's source code, and I checked them before publishing.

articles.title: I Spent 3 Days Debugging a Deploy That Was Never Deploying. Here's the Checklist That Fixed It.
articles.description: Three days. That's how long I spent pushing fixes to a GitHub Pages site that never changed.  Every...
articles.body_html:
Three days. That's how long I spent pushing fixes to a GitHub Pages site that never changed.

Every push succeeded. Every workflow showed green. Every fix worked in my dev environment. And every single time I opened the live URL, the same console error stared back at me:

Failed to load module script: Expected a JavaScript-or-Wasm module script but the server responded with a MIME type of "application/octet-stream"

I'm 13. I built a calorie tracker called ForkCount using AI Studio. The app worked. The deploy didn't. And the worst part wasn't the error — it was that I couldn't tell whether my fixes were failing or whether they were never reaching the browser at all.

Day one, I blamed the build. I rebuilt locally, checked the output, saw that the script tag pointed to a real .js file. The build was fine.

Day two, I blamed GitHub Actions. The workflow looked correct. Green checkmarks everywhere. But the live site was still serving source files instead of the built ones. I didn't understand how both could be true at once.

Day three, I opened my own repo and looked at the docs/ folder. It had assets, it had a .nojekyll file, it had a manifest. It did not have an index.html. The folder I was deploying from was empty of the one file that mattered. GitHub Pages was serving a 404, which fell back to the repo root, which contained my raw source files with /src/main.tsx — a file no browser can execute.

That was the bug. Not the code. Not the workflow. A missing file in a folder I'd looked at ten times without seeing what was absent.

The fix took four commands. Build, copy, add the missing file, push. Three days of debugging ended with a solution so simple I felt stupid for not finding it sooner.

But here's what I actually learned, and it has nothing to do with GitHub Pages:

When something breaks and the fix doesn't work, the first question isn't "what's wrong with the fix?" It's "did the fix actually arrive?" I spent two days debugging code that was never running. Every prompt I sent to my AI assistant went to the source. The source was fine. The source was never the problem.

If you're building something and it keeps failing after every fix, check the layer between your code and your user. Look at what's actually being served, not what you think you deployed. View source. Check the hash. Open the folder. Count the files.

The AI can write the code. It can't see your screen. When something breaks, you have to be the one who notices where the break is.

ForkCount is live now at forkcount.github.io. Free, no card, no trial. I built it because every calorie app I tried hid the math behind a paywall. It still has bugs. But the deploy works, and I know how to check it.

articles.title: LeetCode Made Coding Fun Again
articles.description: Many of us have already fully switched to AI-powered development. We write specs, create skills,...
articles.body_html:
Many of us have already fully switched to AI-powered development. We write specs, create skills, connect MCP and run several agents in the background, after which we do a very boring code review of the result.

For almost all of this year I’ve been writing code with the help of AI, and it’s definitely productive (otherwise I wouldn’t be doing it), but it’s not as fun as it was before. Writing code is like LEGO or puzzles, first you come up with what the solution should look like, then what the first steps should be, and then you write the code, some things work right away, and some things break along the way and you rewrite what doesn’t work. And now imagine if you asked a robot to put a puzzle together for you. It’s put together, the result is there, but did you enjoy it?

I’ve heard an opinion from other developers, “Then write code without AI, what’s the problem?”, but unfortunately it’s not a solution. I think you’ve played computer games like GTA SA, where you can enter the cheat code “HESOYAM” and get a huge amount of money right away. Will you be just as motivated to earn this money in the game honestly, if you’ve used this cheat code once? Most likely not. You’ll consider it a waste of time, because you can just type a command. It’s the same with AI development. It’s very hard to make yourself sit down again and do everything by hand, when you can write a prompt and an AI agent will do it for you.

And for some time it was really sad for me. On the one hand, AI lets us be productive, make PoCs quickly and get rid of boring routine work, but on the other hand it takes away the reason why many of us fell in love with programming.

When I was just starting to learn programming in 2016-2017, I really loved challenges (I still love them, but back then it was especially important). When our C++ teacher gave us a problem on algorithms or data structures, I wanted to do it better and faster than all my classmates. It was a competition. And solving some of the problems took several days (or rather sleepless nights), for example tic-tac-toe where you play against artificial intelligence (so-called, not an LLM), or the 15 puzzle in the console.

When we finished with C++, I switched to Java/C#, where I was focused more on OOP, frameworks and patterns than on algorithms. And after that I never went back to them (except for a few tasks at work, when they really came in handy).

And now, in 2026, I’ve started solving problems on LeetCode, and it has literally taken me back to the time when it was interesting for me to write code where you had to think about algorithms, look for optimal solutions (like O(1) memory and O(n) time), and write everything yourself. Now it has become my hobby.

Some of you might think, “Why doesn’t AI get in the way of enjoying LeetCode too?” On LeetCode nobody needs the finished solution, only the process matters. Asking AI to solve a problem there is like asking a robot to put together a puzzle that you bought for fun.

I ignored LeetCode for a long time, because programming at work was enough for me. Now, when AI writes the code at work, LeetCode has become a place where I can get a challenge again.

As for the platform itself, LeetCode is not the only one you can use (it’s just one of the most popular). You can also use Codeforces, Codewars and so on.

Also, I want to mention “Advent of Code”, which is an annual event (every December) where you solve interesting programming puzzles. Here you move forward through the story and face really varied problems.

A question to my readers, how do you manage to get back the enjoyment of programming?

My blog: https://olegdubovoi.com/
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/olegdubovoi/

articles.title: How I finally understood what idempotency is
articles.description: The Intro   Idempotency. Eight letters, five syllables, and a word I pretended to understand...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Idempotency. Eight letters, five syllables, and a word I pretended to understand in meetings for an embarrassingly long time.

It kept showing up in API docs, in Stripe's dashboard, in that one coworker's code review comments. I nodded. I did not know.

So today we are going to build the bug that makes idempotency matter, charge a fake customer twice, and then fix it. By the end, "idempotent" will be a word you can use in a sentence without sweating.

The What

Here is the dictionary version:

An operation is idempotent if performing it multiple times has the same effect as performing it once.

That's it. No, really, that's the whole concept. The hard part is noticing where it matters.

My favorite non-code example: the elevator button. Press it once, the elevator comes. Press it twelve times because you are late... the elevator still comes once. The button is idempotent. Impatient people everywhere rely on this.

Now compare that to a vending machine button. Press it twice and you get two sodas and one empty wallet. Not idempotent.

Most of your app is an elevator button. Some of it is a vending machine. The trouble starts when a vending machine gets pressed twice by accident.

The How

Let's build a tiny "pay for an order" endpoint with Express and TypeScript. One route, one fake payment provider, zero databases:

// src/server.ts
import express from 'express'

const app = express()
app.use(express.json())

const orders = new Map<string, { total: number; paid: boolean }>()
orders.set('ord_1', { total: 50, paid: false })

async function chargeCard(amount: number) {
  console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  return `ch_${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)}`
}

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true

  res.json({ chargeId })
})

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on :3000'))

Start it with npx tsx src/server.ts and pay for the order:

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay

💳 charged $50

Lovely. Fifty bucks, one charge, everyone's happy. 🎉

Now let's be realistic about the internet. Your frontend sends the request, the server charges the card, and then... the Wi-Fi hiccups. The response never arrives. The frontend (or the HTTP client, or the user mashing the button) does what every client does when it sees a timeout: it retries.

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay
curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay

💳 charged $50
💳 charged $50

Two charges. One order. One customer opening a support ticket with a lot of capital letters. 😬

Our endpoint is a vending machine. Every press costs money. And notice that the client did nothing wrong, retrying on a timeout is the correct thing to do. The endpoint just wasn't ready for it.

Step 1: look before you charge

The cheapest fix is to make the endpoint check its own state first:

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  if (order.paid) {
    return res.json({ chargeId: order.chargeId, alreadyPaid: true })
  }

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true
  order.chargeId = chargeId

  res.json({ chargeId })
})

(Add chargeId?: string to the order type so TypeScript stops yelling.)

Run the double curl again:

💳 charged $50

One charge. The second request got a polite "yep, already done" with the same chargeId as the first. Press the elevator button all you want now.

That's idempotency in one if. The operation "pay order 1" now has the same result whether you call it once or five hundred times.

Step 2: the sneaky gap

Before you ship, let's be honest about a hole. What if the two requests arrive at the same time? Both read paid === false, both charge, both set paid = true. Our if didn't help.

In a real app with a real database you close that gap by making the "check and mark" step atomic. In Postgres that's something like:

UPDATE orders SET paid = true WHERE id = $1 AND paid = false

If that update touches one row, you won the race, go charge the card. If it touches zero rows, someone else got there first, return their result. Same idea as our if, just one that the database enforces so two requests can't both pass.

Step 3: idempotency keys (the grown-up version)

There's one more case the paid flag can't cover: what if the client legitimately wants to pay twice? Say, two different orders that happen to look identical, or a "buy again" button.

The industry answer is an idempotency key. The client generates a random ID per attempt and sends it in a header. The server remembers which keys it has seen:

const seen = new Map<string, unknown>()

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.header('Idempotency-Key')
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key header required' })

  if (seen.has(key)) {
    return res.json(seen.get(key))
  }

  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true

  const response = { chargeId }
  seen.set(key, response)
  res.json(response)
})

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123"
curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123"

💳 charged $50

Same key, one charge, identical response both times. A retry is now safe by design: the client keeps the same key while retrying, and only generates a new one when it genuinely wants a new action.

This is exactly what Stripe, PayPal and friends ask you to send. Now you know why. 🧠

(In production, seen lives in your database or Redis with an expiry, not in a Map. But the shape is the same.)

Step 4: wait, we trust the client to pick the key?

Yep. And it has to be that way. Look at it from the server's side: two identical POST /orders/ord_1/pay requests show up. Is that a flaky network resending one payment, or a customer who genuinely wants to buy twice? The server has no idea. Only the thing that decided to pay knows if it's deciding again. So the client tags the decision, and retries carry the same tag.

What we don't do is trust the client blindly. The server adds a few guardrails:

  • Scope the key to the user. Look it up as (userId, key), not just key. Nobody can replay or collide with someone else's request.
  • Fingerprint the body. Store a hash of the request along with the key. Same key, different body? That's not a retry, that's someone being clever. Answer with a 422.
  • Expire keys. Keep them for a day or so, then forget them. A retry from last month is not a retry.
  • Lock while in flight. If a second request with the same key arrives while the first is still running, make it wait (or return a 409). That also closes the race from Step 2.

With those four, the client can only ever use a key to say "that same thing again, please". Which is exactly what we wanted.

The Why

Let's zoom out, because this is bigger than payments:

  • Retries are everywhere. HTTP clients retry. Message queues redeliver. Users double-click. Cron jobs overlap. If your operation isn't idempotent, every one of those is a bug waiting for a bad Wi-Fi day.
  • Idempotent code is restartable code. A script that imports 10,000 rows and crashes at row 7,000? If each row is an "insert or update", you just run it again. If it's "insert", you now have 7,000 duplicates and a long afternoon.
  • HTTP already has opinions. GET, PUT and DELETE are supposed to be idempotent. POST is not. That's why "create order" is a POST and "set order status" is a PUT. Delete something twice and the second call should say "fine, it's gone" rather than crash.
  • It's a design question, not a library. No package makes your code idempotent. You get it by asking, for every action: "what happens if this runs twice?" and making the answer "nothing new".

The one-sentence version to keep in your pocket: pressing it again should never make things worse.

The Goodbye

Next time someone drops "we should make that idempotent" in a review, you can nod and know. Even better, you can go find the endpoint in your app that charges, emails or creates something, run it twice, and see what happens.

Go press some elevator buttons. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: API key security after the OpenCode Console breach
articles.description: API key security after OpenCode's reported Console breach: affected scope, hosted provider credentials, practical checks and the limits of the public notice.
articles.body_html:
OpenCode reports a security breach affecting 1.4% of its Console users, specifically a subset with external providers linked. The latest edited notice says those users were emailed and the incident is ongoing. For API key security, the useful first question is which component holds the credential. A familiar product name can hide several different answers.

TL;DR

  • The reported percentage is of Console users. Installing the local OpenCode agent alone does not establish inclusion in the affected group.
  • Console's documentation says it stores connected provider credentials and serves requests through a shared gateway. That is the documented architecture; the incident's access path remains undisclosed.
  • Review the official notification and provider activity. Preserving evidence, revoking suspicious credentials and updating affected integrations are general incident-hygiene advice.
  • “Distillation” describes an alleged purpose involving model outputs. The public notice leaves the attacker identity, full customer impact and completed fix open.
  • Sphinx and Pele, two other fresh developer tools, have useful documented boundaries of their own. Read those before adopting either one.

OpenCode Console breach: what the statement actually establishes

The original announcement linked from Hacker News has a newer edited version. The newer statement matters because it spells out a condition that changes how a reader interprets the incident: the affected users had external providers linked. The same statement says OpenCode notified them by email and that users who did not receive an email were not impacted. That is the company's current affected-user claim. It should remain attributed to the company when repeated.

The 1.4% figure needs its denominator attached every time. The population is Console users. The notice does not supply the population's size, so it does not support an absolute victim count. It also does not support applying the percentage to all OpenCode installations, monthly users or GitHub followers. Multiplying two unrelated marketing numbers would make an impressive graphic and an inaccurate one.

The public statement says the team is working with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to remediate. It says details cannot be shared yet because the incident is ongoing. Those are response statements. They leave several ordinary incident questions unanswered: how access was gained, what exact credential handling failed, how much unauthorized activity occurred and which changes will prevent a recurrence.

Individual replies about missing credit or unexpected usage deserve investigation. This article does not independently verify those reports, turn them into a loss total or promise reimbursement. There is no verified reimbursement commitment in the cited notice. A screenshot of somebody's bill would still need an account of what caused the change before it became an incident-wide fact.

We covered the initial announcement as an overnight side story in the previous episode. This is an explicitly requested follow-up, with more room for the scope and documented architecture. My earlier NEEDS REVIEW verdict remains a useful starting position while the technical report is missing.

API key security starts with a credential map

OpenCode's product page describes an open-source coding agent for the terminal, editor and desktop. The Console model documentation describes an optional provider that can be used with OpenCode or another coding agent. A person may use OpenCode with a different provider arrangement. The local agent's name therefore cannot establish whether the person used the affected hosted service.

The Console provider documentation supplies a concrete architectural fact: Console stores a connected provider credential and serves that provider through its gateway. Workspace members can use the models without seeing the upstream provider key. Owners and administrators manage these connections through the Providers tab.

That arrangement has an obvious administrative benefit. A team can share model access without copying an upstream key to every member. It also gives the gateway responsibility for a credential that unlocks an external service. The documented convenience and the documented trust boundary are part of the same design.

A useful inventory separates the pieces:

Piece Question to answer
Local coding agent Which provider configuration does this agent use?
Hosted Console workspace Which external accounts have been connected here?
Provider credential Who can revoke it and where can its activity be inspected?
Downstream integration Which tools depend on this credential being valid?

This is an inventory template. It is not a reconstruction of the attack. Drawing an attacker moving along these boxes would imply knowledge the announcement has not supplied. The exact failure could involve a different part of the service, and the eventual report will have to explain that.

For the same reason, keeping the percentage narrow does not make the impact trivial. A subset can contain people with serious exposure. Scope helps those people find the right response and helps other readers avoid treating an unrelated component as a confirmed victim.

What to check when provider credentials may be exposed

Start with the official notice and your own account arrangement. Establish whether external providers were connected through Console. Review the notification the company says it sent. If something about your account remains unclear, use the official support channel and ask about that concrete configuration rather than trying to diagnose it from another person's reply thread.

Then review provider activity. Preserve the relevant timestamps and records before changing the credential arrangement, where that is practical and consistent with containing suspicious use. If you identify suspicious activity, revoke the exposed credential through the provider that issued it. Update affected integrations with a deliberate replacement rather than leaving a silently failing tool in the background.

These are general incident-response habits, offered as editorial advice. OpenCode's announcement has not published a complete customer remediation checklist. Follow any newer, account-specific instructions that the company and the affected provider supply. The live notice should be rechecked before this piece is published because an ongoing incident can change while a video is being edited.

For future integrations, record where a credential lives, which upstream account it reaches and who owns revocation. Restrict its permissions and spending where the provider supports that. Review activity and keep an inventory of dependencies that will need updating after a replacement. The exact controls depend on the provider and account type; a generic “rotate everything” slogan does not perform that inventory for you.

I would also distinguish the service's access controls from the agent's working permissions. A code-review hook, terminal prompt or confident model answer supplies a different kind of assurance. It does not establish the security of a hosted credential store. Developers already spend enough time asking whether a green badge means what they think it means.

What “distillation attack” tells us

Anthropic's background explanation defines distillation as training a less capable model on the outputs of a stronger one. The technique also has legitimate uses. A provider can distill its own models into smaller versions; unauthorized extraction campaigns use outputs for a different purpose.

OpenCode associates this breach with a large-scale distillation attack. The useful reading is that this describes the alleged purpose of the activity. It leaves the access mechanism open. The words do not identify an attacker, explain how credentials were handled or quantify what happened to customers.

Anthropic's February article discusses separate cases. Its named organizations and account totals must stay attached to those cases. They provide no attribution for this OpenCode incident. A story can have a plausible motive while still lacking a public technical cause, and the two should remain separate fields in the reporting.

The later report should help customers answer what changed in the system they actually used. Until then, an elaborate attack diagram would mainly demonstrate how well the illustrator can connect arrows.

Also today: Sphinx asks you to explain the diff

Sphinx is a Git hook that pauses protected-branch pushes for an understanding check. A separate reviewer reads the committed change without the generating chat. It asks about behavior and failure cases. Its published worker/redelivery conversation is illustrative; we have not installed Sphinx or measured a production-review improvement.

The adoption caveats deserve attention. Installation changes the global Git hook path. The reviewer provider receives changed code and answers. Filename-based exclusions cannot catch a secret embedded in ordinary source. There is no default cap on model calls; a typical check uses five to eight requests plus about one per answer. Local hooks can be bypassed, and the examiner can be wrong. This is an exercise in understanding with costs and data flow to inspect.

Also today: Pele changes the theme while keeping the SVG

Obsidian's kepano released Pele, a Mermaid-to-SVG renderer with CSS-variable theming. Its bundle table reports about 230 kB compressed against Mermaid's 1.6 MB. Speed comparisons remain the project's measurements; we did not reproduce them.

We did make a small behavior check in the real homepage editor. Changing the documented CSS variables preserved the same SVG node and four labels while the computed background and line colors changed. That demonstrates the advertised theme behavior, with no claim about render speed.

The security page says displayed images can make network requests, and the application owns supplied icon markup and internal-link navigation. Links and images can be disabled. Source/output limits are documented. A smaller dependency still arrives with responsibilities for its caller.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I'd keep the Console incident under review until enough information is published to assess the affected credentials and the fix. The practical habit is to identify which service actually holds your provider access. That information remains useful after the current headline leaves the front page.

FAQ

Does using the local OpenCode agent put me in the reported affected group?

Installation alone does not establish that. The official notice names a subset of Console users with external providers linked. Check your own provider arrangement and the company's notification.

Does 1.4% tell us how many people were affected?

The total Console population is undisclosed in the cited notice. An absolute count cannot be calculated from that statement alone.

Has OpenCode published the root cause or completed fix?

The reviewed notice says the incident is ongoing and additional details cannot yet be shared. It states that the team is working with three providers to remediate. It does not establish completion.

Will an AI understanding check secure my provider credentials?

A tool such as Sphinx asks a different question: whether you can explain a committed change. Its own documentation exposes reviewer limitations and data flow. Credential storage needs its own reviewed controls.

Sources

  • Latest edited OpenCode notice
  • OpenCode product
  • Console provider gateway
  • Optional Console models
  • Distillation background
  • Sphinx documentation
  • Pele
  • Pele security
  • Pele maintainer explanation

articles.title: 226 Scenarios, 43 Detectors, 1 Clean Run: Building a Test Harness That Can't Lie
articles.description: The detectors I didn't trust were the ones that stayed quiet. A rule that fires is easy to...
articles.body_html:
The detectors I didn't trust were the ones that stayed quiet. A rule that fires is easy to sanity-check. A rule that does nothing could mean "checked, found nothing," or "crashed before it checked," and from the outside those look the same.

I ended up with 43 detectors in agentwatch, part of the agentic-suite suite, and this is the harness I built to stop confusing the two. It runs 226 scenarios in about twelve seconds.

The shape of a scenario

Every case is a small dataclass that knows how to build a trace and what should happen to it:

@dataclass
class Scenario:
    id: str
    detector: type
    expect_fire: bool
    build: Callable                     # -> (RunSummary, list[SpanNode])
    severity: str | None = None
    pool: dict[str, Any] | None = None  # scripted DB values
    phase: str = "matrix"               # matrix | precision | llm | clean

The traces are built by hand, not sampled from a corpus, so there's exactly one thing being tested at a time:

add("L1", LoopDetector, True,
    lambda: (summ(total_tool_calls=6), [tool("search_kb") for _ in range(6)]),
    severity="warning")

Six identical calls, threshold of five, should fire a warning. No ambiguity to argue about later.

The traces are hand-built for a reason. A corpus tells you whether the detector fires on real data, but it can't tell you whether it fires for the right reason — corpus traces don't have ground-truth labels. A hand-built trace has exactly one property being tested, and the expected outcome is known before the detector runs. That's the only layer that can compute true TPR and FPR.

Faking the database

Six detectors query Postgres for baselines. Rather than spin up Postgres for the tests, they query a dict:

class ScriptedPool:
    def __init__(self, values=None):
        self.conn = _Conn(values or {})
    def acquire(self):
        return _Acq(self.conn)

The trick is in how the detectors decide whether they have a real pool. _has_valid_pool() checks for an acquire method and not a Mock's return_value — a heuristic that distinguishes a real asyncpg pool from a unittest.mock.Mock. ScriptedPool has acquire but no return_value, so it passes for the real thing and the detectors run their async queries against a dictionary. No Docker, no Postgres, no asyncpg — and about a thousand times faster than spinning up a database container.

The detectors check for an acquire method and not a Mock's return_value, so a ScriptedPool passes for the real thing and runs its async queries against a dictionary.

add("CV1", CostVsBaselineDetector, True,
    lambda: (summ(agent_version="v1", estimated_cost=6.0), []),
    severity="warning", pool={"avg_cost": 2.5})   # baseline $2.50, run $6.00

No Docker, no Postgres, and about a thousand times faster.

Real calls, not mocks

The twelve LLM scenarios hit a real model. This matters, because a mock always returns something valid and can never show you an endpoint that's down — which is exactly the bug that had been hiding in my suite for weeks. So each scenario snapshots the client's counters before and after:

stats_before = dict(client._stats)
anomaly = await det.detect_async(summary, spans, pool=None)
stats_after = dict(client._stats)

llm_calls = stats_after["chat_calls"] - stats_before["chat_calls"]
embed_calls = stats_after["embed_calls"] - stats_before["embed_calls"]

That delta is what lets the harness ask the question that matters.

Six checks, not one

Most detector suites check one thing. This one checks six: did it fire, was the severity right, was it the right detector, was there an explanation, was there an evidence dict, and — the one I care about most — was the model actually called.

tip: A negative case where the model was never called is not a pass. It's a skip wearing a pass. Assert that the dependency ran, not just that the output looked right.

There's a seventh for LLM cases too: parse the model's JSON and confirm its verdict matches what was expected, so a detector can't fire for the wrong reason. For a positive case, the model should say {"hallucination": true}. For a negative, {"hallucination": false}. If the detector fires but the model's verdict disagrees, the detector has a logic bug — it fired for the wrong reason. Verdict matching catches that.

The phase design

The 226 scenarios split into four phases, each catching a different class of bug:

Phase Cases What it catches
matrix 166 (154 ported + 12 hook patterns) Per-detector fire/no-fire and severity
precision 48 (n−1 vs n for 24 thresholds) Off-by-one and floating-point at boundaries
llm 12 (6 LLM detectors, real calls) Silent skips, verdict mismatches
clean 1 (43 detectors, 1 normal trace) False positives on clean input

The matrix phase is the ported predecessor suite — 154 scenarios from the original 35-detector field-test plan, plus 12 new Claude Code hook-pattern detectors. These are the "does it fire when it should" cases, and they're the layer most suites stop at.

The precision phase exists because numeric thresholds live at the boundary. Testing only at n+5 misses off-by-one errors; testing only at n hits floating-point. Two cases per threshold — one below, one at the line — catch both. Forty-eight cases across twenty-four thresholds, and that's the layer that caught the 6/9 ÷ 3/9 = 1.9999... floating-point bug.

The LLM phase is the one that needs real calls, and the one the llm_called_ok check lives in. Mocks would make this phase pass vacuously — a mock always returns a valid response, so a detector that silently fails looks like it works.

The clean phase is one case — all 43 detectors against a single known-normal trace, expecting zero fires. It's the cheapest test in the harness and the most valuable, and it gets its own article in this series.

Boundary cases

For every numeric threshold, two cases — one just below and one at the line:

prec("P-loop-4", LoopDetector, False, _tools(["search_kb"] * 4))              # under
prec("P-loop-5", LoopDetector, True,  _tools(["search_kb"] * 5), "warning")   # at
prec("P-cost-500", CostSpikeDetector, False, lambda: (summ(estimated_cost=5.0), []))
prec("P-cost-501", CostSpikeDetector, True,  lambda: (summ(estimated_cost=5.01), []))

The CostSpikeDetector uses a strict > comparison, so 5.0 doesn't fire (not > 5.0) and 5.01 does. Testing at exactly 5.0 confirms the strictness; testing at 5.01 confirms the threshold. Without both, a >= that should be > slips through.

tip: Test at n−1 and at n for every numeric threshold. The exact boundary is where off-by-one and floating-point bugs live. A test at n+5 proves the detector can fire; it says nothing about where the threshold actually is.

The clean-run check

All 43 detectors against a single known-normal trace, expecting zero fires. The clean trace has three different tools, one-second gaps, a success status, twelve cents of cost, and a 200-character output — every value far from every threshold. If anything fires, it's a false positive, full stop.

async def run_clean():
    summary, spans = _clean_trace()
    fired = [det.anomaly_type
             for det in create_all_detectors()
             if await det.detect_async(summary, spans, pool=None) is not None]
    return {"detectors": 43, "fired": fired, "ok": not fired}

It comes back empty. The full story of why this check matters — and the predecessor data that made it non-negotiable — is in the next piece in this series.

Why it holds up

The rule-based cases run in about four milliseconds. The twelve model calls take a second each and dominate the total, which is still fine for CI. The whole thing ends at 226 of 226, with a hundred percent true-positive rate and zero false positives on the clean trace.

The severity distribution across the matrix cases: 47 warning, 26 critical, 4 info, 77 silent (no anomaly). Every severity matched. The LLM telemetry across the 12 real-call scenarios: 12 chat calls, 100% JSON parse success, latency p50 ≈ 606 ms, p99 ≈ 1427 ms. All LLM request/response I/O is captured in llm-scenario-io.jsonl — 13 records with prompts, system messages, raw responses, model names, and timing. That's the audit trail: the exact thing the model said for each scenario, preserved.

The design choices that did the work were unglamorous: hand-built traces instead of a corpus, a fake database instead of a real one, real model calls instead of mocks, two cases per threshold, and the boring clean trace almost nobody writes.

The harness is checked in at scenario_validation.py. The full results are in detector-results.json.

The design question worth asking of any detector suite: does it check that the dependency ran, or just that the output looked right? The first can't be satisfied by accident. The second can — and that's where silent failures hide.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.1.0 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools
  • Field test report (FT-15, 226 scenarios)
  • Detector results: detector-results.json

articles.title: Exact-Match Edits vs Patches: How Claude Code, Codex and Aider Write to Your Files
articles.description: Claude Code's Edit refuses a duplicate match; Codex's apply_patch and Aider's SEARCH/REPLACE take the first one. How each edit protocol fails.
articles.body_html:
• Book: Prompt Engineering Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your config file has two functions that both set timeout = 30. You ask a coding agent to raise the production timeout to 60. Depending on which agent you asked, one of two things happens. The edit is refused until the agent adds more context. Or the first timeout = 30 in the file changes, which is the development one, and the patch applies cleanly.

The edit protocol decides that outcome: the format the agent uses to describe a change, and the code on your machine that applies it. Claude Code, Codex and Aider each use a different one, and their docs and source say exactly what happens when the text doesn't line up.

Here is the file used for every case below:

def load_dev():
    timeout = 30
    retries = 3

def load_prod():
    timeout = 30
    retries = 5

Three ways to say "change this line"

Claude Code: exact string replacement. The Edit tool takes an old_string and a new_string and, in the docs' words, "doesn't use regex or fuzzy matching." Three checks must pass: Claude has read the file, old_string appears exactly as written, and it appears exactly once unless replace_all: true is set. The read rule is looser for newer models. The same page says Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5 and older models always require the read, while newer models on Claude Code v2.1.208 or later can skip it when the Read tool is available and reading wouldn't need a permission prompt.

The documented fields, for our task:

Edit
  old_string: "    timeout = 30"
  new_string: "    timeout = 60"
  replace_all: false

Codex: patch envelopes. OpenAI's Codex Prompting Guide tells you to use apply_patch for single-file edits, says the model "has been trained to excel at this diff format", and strongly recommends using OpenAI's exact implementation. That implementation is open source in the codex-rs/apply-patch crate. Its markers are *** Begin Patch, *** Add File:, *** Delete File:, *** Update File:, *** Move to:, *** End of File, @@ and *** End Patch. Changed lines start with - or +, context lines with a space, and there are no line numbers:

*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: config.py
@@
-    timeout = 30
+    timeout = 60
*** End Patch

Aider: you pick the format. Aider's edit formats include whole (the model returns the entire file), diff (SEARCH/REPLACE blocks), diff-fenced (the same blocks with the path inside the fence, mainly for Gemini models), udiff (a simplified unified diff) and two editor- variants for architect mode. A diff block looks like a merge conflict:

config.py
```python
<<<<<<< SEARCH
    timeout = 30
=======
    timeout = 60
>>>>>>> REPLACE
```

Aider also publishes how often models get the format right. Its polyglot leaderboard, last updated November 20, 2025, puts a "Correct edit format" column next to the pass rate over 225 exercises. gpt-5 (high) tops the table at 88.0% correct, with 91.6% on edit format using diff. Even the top model sent a malformed edit in some cases, and the applier has to catch each one.

The duplicate line: one refuses, two pick the first

Claude Code's uniqueness check fails, because timeout = 30 appears twice. Per the docs, Claude then "either supplies a longer string with enough surrounding context to pin down one occurrence, or sets replace_all: true to replace them all." The retry that works carries the function header:

Edit
  old_string: "def load_prod():\n    timeout = 30"
  new_string: "def load_prod():\n    timeout = 60"
  replace_all: false

Codex's applier doesn't check uniqueness. In file_update.rs, each chunk's old lines are searched from the current position forward, and seek_sequence.rs returns the first window that matches without looking at later ones. With the bare @@ patch above, the first timeout = 30 sits in load_dev. That line changes.

The anchor fixes it. Text after @@ is a change context: the applier finds that line first and only searches for the old lines after it.

*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: config.py
@@ def load_prod():
-    timeout = 30
+    timeout = 60
*** End Patch

Aider's diff format behaves like Codex here. In editblock_coder.py, perfect_replace replaces the first block of lines that matches and returns. One path is stricter. When a SEARCH block uses ... to elide lines, Aider refuses the block if that chunk appears more than once.

To be fair to Codex and Aider, models rarely send one bare line. Context lines in a patch and a multi-line SEARCH block usually make the match unique anyway. The difference shows up when they don't: Claude Code stops, the other two apply at the first match.

Stale context: the file moved since the model looked

The model's copy of a file goes stale when you edit it, a formatter runs, or a second agent touches it.

Claude Code has a documented rule for this case. Since v2.1.208, if the file changed after Claude's last read but old_string still matches the current content "exactly and unambiguously" and the file is readable without a prompt, the edit applies and the result notes that the file carries other changes, so Claude re-reads before edits that depend on the surrounding code. In any other case, such as a stale old_string, Claude reads the file again before editing. Before v2.1.208 it refused any edit to a file that changed on disk after the read.

Codex fails with a message the model can act on. If the @@ line isn't found, file_update.rs returns Failed to find context '<line>' in <path>. If the old lines aren't found, it returns Failed to find expected lines in <path>: followed by the lines it looked for. The API guide describes the same loop for your own harness: report status: "failed" with a short human-readable message.

Aider replies with SearchReplaceNoExactMatch: This SEARCH block failed to exactly match lines in <path>, plus the reminder that "The SEARCH section must exactly match an existing block of lines including all white space, comments, indentation, docstrings, etc". If misses keep coming, its troubleshooting page suggests, among other things, --edit-format whole.

The whole format can't miss a match, because there is nothing to match. If the model's copy of the file was old, though, the rewrite puts that old version back over whatever changed since, and nothing reports an error. The other risk is elision. The edit-formats page says udiff was mainly used with GPT-4 Turbo because it reduced that model's habit of eliding code with comments like "original code here". In Aider's unified diffs write-up, moving GPT-4 Turbo from SEARCH/REPLACE to udiff raised its laziness benchmark score from 20% to 61%.

Whitespace drift: strict, forgiving, and in between

Models re-type the text they want to replace, and re-typing drifts. A tab comes back as four spaces, trailing whitespace disappears, a straight quote turns curly.

Claude Code is strict on purpose. The docs say "A single character of whitespace or indentation difference is enough to miss." When it misses, the edit doesn't apply.

Codex's applier is the most forgiving of the three. seek_sequence makes four passes in what its comment calls "decreasing strictness": an exact match, then ignoring trailing whitespace, then trimming both sides, then normalising common Unicode punctuation like dashes and quotes to ASCII. Indentation drift in the old lines still finds its target. The price shows up when nothing matches exactly. A looser pass can match in more places, and the first window it finds wins.

Aider sits in between. It tries an exact match, then a match that tolerates missing leading whitespace, then retries without a stray blank first line. A fuzzy edit-distance matcher exists in the same file, but a bare return sits in front of the call, so it never runs.

Leniency pays off. The same unified diffs write-up reports that turning flexible patching off produced "a 9X increase in editing errors".

Failure Claude Code Edit Codex apply_patch Aider diff
Duplicate match Refused First match after anchor First match
Stale text Applies if still exact, else re-reads Error to model Error to model
Whitespace drift Miss Four lenient passes Tolerates leading whitespace

An undo that doesn't care how the bytes got there

Every failure above has a quiet version: the edit applies in the wrong place, or on top of stale assumptions, and the agent reports success. You catch it in review, and then you want that one turn back.

Each tool has its own answer. Claude Code's checkpoints capture your code before each prompt, and /rewind restores code, conversation or both. The docs are clear about the edge: "Checkpointing does not track files modified by Bash commands", and most subagent edits aren't restored either. Aider commits every edit to git with a descriptive message, and /undo discards the last change. Each one covers its own agent's edits and nothing else.

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this with that in mind. Hermes runs Claude Code, Codex, Aider and other agents, each in its own terminal, and saves every agent turn, so you can diff or restore any single turn, with undo (README). The strip under a session lists the agent's replies with the lines each changed. Click one to see its changes or restore your files to that point (2.3.1 notes). The Review Desk (⌘G) shows the same work by turn or by file.


The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view for a Claude Code task: two turns, turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, the changed files, and a commit message drafted from the turns.

Because the snapshot is of your files, not of the edit calls, the same restore works for every agent, whether the change arrived as an old_string, a patch envelope or a SEARCH block. There are two limits. In a Claude Code task with extra folders, the strip tracks the main project only (2.3.1 notes). Turn snapshots from tasks that ran in their own worktree are removed 14 days after the session closes (2.2.9 notes).

What to do with this

If you run Codex or Aider on files with repeated blocks, like per-environment config or test tables, check where the diff landed, not only what it says.

If Claude Code keeps missing an edit, look for mixed tabs and spaces or invisible characters in the file before you blame the model. If you use Aider's whole format, keep other writers off that file while the agent works, because a rewrite from a stale copy applies without an error.

Whatever the protocol, keep a per-turn record outside the edit path: plain commits, Aider's auto-commit, or a turn snapshot.

If this was useful

An edit format is structured output with a strict parser on the other end, and Aider's leaderboard shows that even top models miss the format in some share of cases. If you write prompts that ask a model for output a program has to parse, the Prompt Engineering Pocket Guide is my short book on prompting techniques, structured output among them. If you run several of these agents side by side, Hermes IDE is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and lives on GitHub.

articles.title: HisabMate: A Local-First, AI-Assisted Digital Bahi-Khata for Indian Microbusinesses
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

HisabMate is a local-first, AI-assisted bahi-khata (the traditional credit ledger) for Indian microbusinesses.

If you have ever bought something from a neighbourhood kirana, a tailor, or a small wholesaler, you have probably seen the system: a notebook where the owner writes who owes what. Customers take goods on credit (udhaar), pay back in pieces, and the owner reconciles it all by hand. It works because it is simple, but it is also fragile. Pages get smudged, entries go missing, and a disputed balance turns into an argument between two people who both want to stay on good terms.

Many bookkeeping tools exist, but they often assume cloud accounts, subscriptions, and a comfort with accounting vocabulary that a busy shopkeeper may not have. HisabMate takes a narrower path: keep the ledger on the owner's own machine, make the arithmetic exact and boring, and let a local language model help with the typing, never with the money.

The person who would pay for something like this is the owner who already runs on credit and handwritten pages and wants a clearer, searchable, exportable record without handing customer data to a third party. To be upfront: I have not had a paying user yet, so that is my hypothesis about the market, not a result.

Demo

HisabMate is not deployed publicly. It runs locally, and the two screenshots below are from the real application running on localhost.

Screenshot 1: HisabMate running locally at http://127.0.0.1:5174/.

Screenshot 2: a second view of the working local application.

Code

sm4006 / HisabMate

HisabMate

HisabMate is a local-first AI-assisted bahi-khata for Indian microbusinesses The Python backend owns validation, integer-paise calculations, SQLite persistence, idempotency, and CSV export. The React frontend is a local dashboard and review workflow.

Requirements

  • Python 3.10+ (Python 3.13+ is the target documented in the PRD)
  • Node.js and npm
  • Optional: Ollama for natural-language transaction proposals

No Python package installation is required: the backend uses the standard library. Frontend dependencies are declared in frontend/package.json.

Installation

From the repository root:

Set-Location .\frontend
npm install
Set-Location ..

The backend creates the SQLite schema automatically on first start. It does not seed customers or transactions.

Ollama setup

Install Ollama separately, start its local service, and install the configured model:

ollama pull llama3.2:3b

HisabMate uses llama3.2:3b by default through http://localhost:11434. Override the model or endpoint when needed:

$env:OLLAMA_MODEL = "llama3.2:3b"
$env:OLLAMA_HOST = "http://localhost:11434"

The…

View on GitHub

Repository: github.com/sm4006/HisabMate

How I Built It

Architecture

The design rule is that the model proposes and the code decides.

  • Backend (Python, standard library only). It owns validation, integer-paise calculations, SQLite persistence, idempotency, and CSV export. There are no Python packages to install.
  • Frontend (React). A local dashboard and review workflow that talks to the backend API at http://127.0.0.1:8000/api.
  • AI layer (Ollama). HisabMate uses llama3.2:3b by default through a local Ollama service at http://localhost:11434. The model and endpoint can be overridden with the OLLAMA_MODEL and OLLAMA_HOST environment variables.
  • Storage. A local SQLite database. The schema is created automatically on first start, and nothing is seeded.

Safeguards documented in the repository

Money software has to be dull in the right places, so these are the parts I care about most:

  • Integer paise, never floats. Credit and payment amounts are stored as integer paise, with exact two-decimal rupee/paise input validation. Balances are deterministic.
  • Model output is a proposal only. When Ollama interprets a natural-language entry, the response goes through strict validation in Python. Nothing is written to the ledger until the user explicitly confirms it.
  • Idempotent confirmations. Confirmed transaction submissions use persistent idempotency, so a double click or a retry does not create a duplicate entry.
  • Append-only corrections. Mistakes are corrected by adding a new entry with an audit reference, not by silently editing history, much like striking through a line in a paper ledger.
  • Safer CSV export. Text fields that begin with spreadsheet formula characters are escaped, so an exported file does not turn a customer name into a formula.
  • Honest empty fields. The CSV has a remarks column, but the current schema stores no remarks, so it is exported blank rather than guessed.

What works today

  • Customer records with outstanding balances calculated from the ledger.
  • Credit and payment transactions.
  • Local Ollama transaction proposals with an explicit confirmation step.
  • Customer-specific ledgers and a Daily Hisab view filtered by business date, customer, transaction type, and search text.
  • Transaction-history CSV export that respects the active filters.
  • Loading, empty, validation, offline, and API-error states in the frontend.
  • A Python unittest suite, a compile check, and a frontend build, all runnable from the README commands.

How GitHub Copilot fits in

I used GitHub Copilot Chat in VS Code, primarily in Agent mode, as a coding assistant throughout HisabMate's development.

I used it to help implement and refine the Python ledger and API, build the React/Vite interface, develop the AI-assisted transaction proposal flow, add Daily Hisab filters and CSV export, and expand tests and project documentation. I worked incrementally, reviewing the implementation and testing the application between tasks.

One concrete moment where it helped: Copilot helped connect the customer-specific ledger view to the backend so that selecting a customer displayed that customer's transactions and outstanding balance rather than generic or unrelated data.

One moment that required correction: During the final submission process, I had to correct the Git remote configuration before the existing local commit could be pushed to GitHub. This was a reminder that agent-generated instructions still need to be checked against the actual repository state.

What remained human-owned: The core financial-safety decisions were not delegated to the model. Transaction amounts use integer paise, the backend validates proposed transactions, and the user must review and explicitly confirm a transaction before it is written to the ledger. The AI proposes an interpretation; it does not get direct database-write authority.

I also reviewed the generated changes, ran tests and build checks, and checked the application against the intended workflow rather than treating generated code as automatically correct.

Repository: https://github.com/sm4006/HisabMate

Copilot was a development aid, not a substitute for reviewing financial logic or verifying the finished application.

Known Limitations

I would rather list these here than have a reader discover them:

  • No contact details or opening balances. The current SQLite schema does not represent them.
  • No free-text remarks. They are not stored, so search covers customer names and controlled transaction labels only.
  • Out of scope for this release: payment reminders, CSV customization, bank integrations, and multi-user accounts.
  • No frontend unit or end-to-end test framework. The browser workflows were manually exercised against disposable local services, and the Python suite is the automated safety net.
  • Ollama must be installed and running for live interpretation. The normal Python test suite does not need it.
  • A 3B model is small. I am not publishing accuracy benchmarks for its interpretations. That is exactly why every proposal needs a human confirmation before it touches the ledger.
  • Setup instructions in the README use PowerShell syntax. Other shells will need small adjustments.
  • Not deployed. There is no hosted version. It is meant to run on the owner's own machine.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a small business, a ledger is not just data. It is who trusts whom, and how much. Open-weight models and local inference change what is possible here:

  1. The data can stay on the owner's machine. By default, HisabMate points at a local Ollama endpoint and a local SQLite file. A closed hosted API would mean sending customer names and amounts to a server the shopkeeper does not control.
  2. The cost model fits the customer. A microbusiness cannot easily absorb per-request fees or a monthly subscription for something that used to be a notebook. Running a model locally has no per-call bill.
  3. The model is swappable. Because the model name and host are configuration, not a vendor contract, the owner or a local developer can try a different open model without rewriting the application.
  4. The behaviour is inspectable. The backend is plain Python and the rules that guard the money are readable. For software that tracks who owes whom, being able to read the rules is a feature.

The honest trade-off is capability. A small local model is weaker than a large hosted one, which is why HisabMate treats it as a typing assistant behind a validation boundary rather than as an authority.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot

Thanks for reading, and for any feedback, especially from anyone who has run a credit-based shop and knows what a real bahi-khata needs.

articles.description: HustlePilot: an AI copilot for small businesses that is not allowed to invent...
articles.body_html:
HustlePilot: an AI copilot for small businesses that is not allowed to invent numbers

Draft DEV post for Hacktoberfest 2026. AI disclosure: this project and this draft were built with agent assistance (some_ai).

Small sellers — a plant nursery in this case — already have data: WhatsApp order notes, a sales CSV, a products sheet. What they don't have is time to read it every morning. HustlePilot is a local-first AI copilot that turns three CSVs into a ranked morning briefing: what's running low, what's slowing down, which inquiries went cold, and which listings are thin.

The interesting part isn't the LLM. It's the rules around it.

The one design rule: code computes, the LLM writes

Every number you see in HustlePilot — stock cover, sales rate ratios, days waiting on an inquiry — is computed by deterministic pandas rules (backend/app/services/analytics.py). The LLM's only job is to turn that evidence into a sentence a human would write.

And it may only reuse numbers that appear in the evidence. Before any narrative reaches the UI, a grounding validator (backend/app/services/grounding.py) extracts every number from the LLM's text and checks it against the evidence dict:

def safe_narrative(opp_type, evidence, llm_text, extra=None):
    """Return (narrative, source, rejected_numbers)."""
    if llm_text:
        bad = ungrounded_numbers(llm_text, evidence, extra)
        if not bad:
            return llm_text.strip(), "llm", []
        return TEMPLATES[opp_type], "template", sorted(bad)
    return TEMPLATES[opp_type], "template", []

If the model says "you sold 94 units last week" and the evidence says 14, the whole narrative is replaced with a boring-but-true template, the rejection is counted, and the UI labels the source (llm vs template). The model can't quietly delete a bad number — the entire text is forfeited. That's on purpose: partial edits are harder to audit than all-or-nothing fallback.

This mirrors a pattern the community keeps re-learning: search-enabled or retrieval-enabled LLMs still get numbers wrong, because retrieval fixes access to facts, not faithfulness in restating them (Why Search-Enabled LLMs Still Get Numbers Wrong 👤 @yany-henry). A validator at the output boundary is the part that actually enforces it (Why your AI agent keeps hallucinating financial data (and how to fix it) 👤 @valyuai).

Screenshots

Architecture in one screen

  • Backend: FastAPI + SQLite (single file, tenant-scoped rows with a business_id, demo API-key auth — it's a single-tenant demo, not multi-tenant SaaS).
  • LLM: any Ollama-compatible endpoint (gemma3:4b locally) or a deterministic mock. Every provider response is labeled real/mock in the UI. No GPU required; inference runs CPU-bound on a laptop.
  • Frontend: React + Vite + Tailwind. Dashboard, CSV import with validation reports, opportunity feed, listing studio, inquiry inbox, approvals queue (draft → approved → exported), history timeline.
  • Eval harness (eval/run_eval.py): five stages — CSV-defect injection, a hand-computed rules fixture, grounding unit checks, labeled inquiry classification vs. a keyword baseline, and latency.

The approval queue matters more than it sounds. Generated drafts never send themselves: an inquiry reply or listing draft sits as submitted until the owner approves, edits, or dismisses it. Every state change is audited.

What the eval actually measured

Honest numbers, with sample sizes:

Stage Result
CSV validation, 30 injected defects 30/30 detected, 0 errors on clean files
Rules fixture (hand-computed expectations) 14/14 checks pass
Grounding unit checks 7/7 (fabricated numbers rejected, ratio edge cases, URL flagging)
Backend tests (pytest, mock providers) 35 passed
API smoke (end-to-end through HTTP) 36/36 checks pass
Real-model latency (gemma3:4b, CPU, n=1) analyze ≈ 77 s · listing ≈ 50 s · inquiry ≈ 56 s

What was not measured, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise: listing-copy quality has no human rating yet; classification accuracy against the labeled fixture is a small-n, single-domain test; and the before/after comparison view in the app is correlational — nothing in HustlePilot claims an action caused a sale. The rules carry honest limitations text on every opportunity for exactly this reason.

Small things that saved the demo

  • AS_OF is derived from max(sale_date), not today's clock — demos are reproducible, and "days waiting" doesn't drift between rehearsals.
  • Slow-mover analysis refuses to run with fewer than recent + baseline days of history (112 by default) and says so in a notice, instead of quietly computing nonsense on two weeks of data.
  • Mock everything, label everything. LLM_PROVIDER=mock and SEARCH_PROVIDER=mock make the full stack testable in CI, and the UI never lets a mock output masquerade as a real one.
  • >20% invalid rows rejects the whole CSV with an explanation, rather than importing the silent majority.

Run it 

# backend
cd backend && pip install -r requirements.txt
cp ../.env.example ../.env   # LLM_PROVIDER=ollama, SEARCH_PROVIDER=mock
uvicorn app.main:app --reload

# frontend
cd frontend && npm install && npm run dev   # proxies /api → :8000

# tests + eval
LLM_PROVIDER=mock SEARCH_PROVIDER=mock pytest -q
python eval/run_eval.py --stage validation --llm mock
python eval/run_eval.py --stage classification --llm real --limit 12

Hit Import sample data in the UI to load a fictional Bengaluru plant nursery (8 products, 619 sales, 5 inquiries).

TL;DR

An LLM that writes your morning briefing is a liability. An LLM that writes your morning briefing under a numeric grounding check, behind an approval queue, with every fallback visible in the UI is a tool. Code computes; the LLM narrates; the human decides.

Built for Hacktoberfest 2026. Feedback, PRs, and "you should have used X instead" all welcome.
