articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

https://voice-order-taker-jvh7zuvem9z6qbfuqfcvpm.streamlit.app/

What I Built

Voice Order Taker is a local app that turns WhatsApp voice notes into a clean order sheet.

In Pakistan, a lot of home businesses run on voice notes. A baker, a tiffin cook or a small clothing seller gets messages like "do kilo chocolate cake aur teen dozen samosay kal shaam tak, house 12 Jinnah Road", in Urdu, Roman Urdu, Pashto or a mix with English. The seller replays each note, then writes the order down by hand. With 20 or more orders a week, that is hours of work, and one misheard quantity means a wrong delivery.

With my app, the seller uploads the voice notes and the app:

  1. Transcribes each note with Whisper.
  2. Extracts customer, item, quantity, unit, delivery date, address and notes with a Gemma model.
  3. Shows an editable order table, a CSV download, and a daily prep list that adds up how many of each item are due on each date.

The person who would pay for this is a home seller handling a steady stream of orders. They don't need a big business tool. They need something that saves an hour a day and doesn't send their customers' addresses to a stranger's server.

Demo

https://youtu.be/0M2gG12_r24

Code

laiba-Ashfaq / voice-order-taker

Voice Order Taker

https://voice-order-taker-jvh7zuvem9z6qbfuqfcvpm.streamlit.app/

Turn WhatsApp voice notes in Urdu, Roman Urdu, Pashto or English into a clean order sheet and a daily prep list. Everything runs on your own computer. No cloud, no API key, no per-order cost.

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge (Week 2: Side Hustle).

The problem

Home bakers, tiffin services and small clothing sellers take most of their orders as WhatsApp voice notes. Someone says "do kilo chocolate cake aur teen dozen samosay kal shaam tak, house 12 Jinnah Road", and the seller has to replay it and write it down by hand. With 20 or more orders a week, this takes hours and mistakes happen.

What it does

  1. You upload one or more voice notes (.ogg, .opus, .m4a, .mp3, .wav).
  2. Whisper transcribes each note locally.
  3. A Gemma model running in Ollama extracts structured orders: customer, item, quantity…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Everything runs on a normal laptop with no cloud service.

  • faster-whisper (open-source Whisper) transcribes audio on the CPU. It reads WhatsApp .opus, .ogg and .m4a files directly.
  • Gemma, running locally through Ollama, reads the transcript and returns structured orders.
  • Streamlit is the interface, with a custom dark navy and teal theme and a CSS-only 3D robot mascot (no images or external libraries, so it works offline too).
  • pandas handles the editable table, the CSV export and the daily prep list.

The most important part was making a small model reliable. A free-form prompt gave me bad results, so I forced the output into a fixed JSON schema and added a worked example inside the prompt:

class OrderLine(BaseModel):
    customer: str = ""
    item: str = ""
    quantity: float = 1
    unit: str = ""
    delivery_date: str = ""
    address: str = ""
    notes: str = ""

class OrderList(BaseModel):
    orders: list[OrderLine]

r = ollama.chat(
    model=model,
    format=OrderList.model_json_schema(),
    options={"temperature": 0, "num_ctx": 2048},
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": system},
              {"role": "user", "content": transcript}],
)

The prompt also converts words like "kal" (tomorrow) and "parson" (day after tomorrow) into real dates, and I give Whisper a short list of dish names as an initial_prompt so it recognises local food words.

What went wrong along the way. I built this on a laptop with a nearly full C: drive and limited RAM, which turned out to be good testing for a "runs on cheap hardware" project:

  • The first model download failed because the disk was full, so I moved the model and cache folders to another drive.
  • A 6.6 GB Gemma model ran out of memory while Whisper was also loaded, so I switched to a smaller Gemma and reduced the context size.
  • A newer audio library version broke Whisper's decoder, so I pinned av<17.
  • My first extraction attempt with the smallest model returned a quantity with no item name. The schema and the worked example fixed most of that.

[Add your real numbers here, for example: "I tested X voice notes. N came out fully correct, M needed one edit, and K failed. Average time per note was about Y seconds on CPU."]

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For this kind of customer, open models are not a nice extra. They are what makes the product possible.

  • Privacy. A voice note contains a customer's name, address and what they bought. With a closed API, all of that goes to a third-party server. Here it never leaves the seller's laptop.
  • Cost. Transcription and extraction cost nothing per order. A home baker can't justify per-minute and per-token fees, and a small flat monthly price still leaves a margin.
  • Offline use. Power and internet outages are common where I live. The app keeps working because nothing depends on a connection after the one-time model download.
  • Control. I could change the prompt, give Whisper local dish names, shrink the context, and swap one Gemma size for another when my laptop couldn't handle the bigger one. With a closed API, I would have been stuck with whatever the provider supports and charges.

The trade-off is honest too: a small local model is less accurate than a large cloud model on messy mixed-language speech, so the app always shows an editable table and the seller confirms the result before acting on it.

articles.title: I fine-tuned Qwen3.6 on Tinker to read my neighbours’ khata: 98% credit/payment accuracy for $0.38
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

My neighbours run a grocery shop. Like thousands of small shops, they sell a lot on credit and keep track in a khata: a paper ledger where every row is a customer, a date, an item, and either udhar (the customer took goods on credit) or jama (they paid something back).
It works until you need an answer. Who owes what? Who hasn't paid in over a month? The answer is somewhere in the pages, and finding it means turning them over by hand.

So I built Ledgerly. You photograph a page. A vision model reads every row. You get a review screen with your photo beside the extracted rows, fix whatever it got wrong, confirm, and the app keeps running balances per customer, with an aging report: who is over 30 days.

The part I care about most is the loop. Every page you confirm carries your corrections, and those corrections are the training data for the next fine-tune (python ft/train.py --from-db). Using the app produces training data.

It reads Hindi (Devanagari), English, and the mixed pages that real ledgers actually are.

Demo

The demo covers gemma running locally and extracting entries from a handwritten ledger page and other functionalities of Ledgerly web app.

What my neighbours said

I asked my neighbours to try it. They found the screens easy to understand almost immediately: the photo next to the rows, the big buttons, the "owes money" and "over 30 days" filters. Their own khata is laid out differently from the pages I trained on, so they couldn't run their book through it yet. They told me they would definitely use it if I rolled it out as an app.

That told me what to build next. The model has to learn their page, and that is what fine-tuning is for: photograph a few pages, label them, and train again for about forty cents.

The side hustle

Who would pay: small shops that sell on credit and still run their books on paper, like my neighbours. They don't need another accounting suite. They need to stop turning pages to find out who owes what.

What I'd sell: the model and the pipeline are open and stay free. I'd charge for the convenience: a hosted version where the shopkeeper photographs a page and the ledger is ready, plus the part that matters most, teaching the model that shop's own page layout. My neighbours' khata looks different from mine, so a one-time setup is exactly what they need: a few photographed and labelled pages, then a fine-tune. The compute for my 9-page run cost about forty cents.

Pricing:: I asked my neighbours what would feel fair for an app like this, and they said ₹100 to ₹150 a month. So I'd offer a free tier of about 20 pages a month, so a shop can try it on its own khata, then roughly ₹120-₹130 a month per shop. A one-time setup would teach the model that shop's own page layout. That's a few rupees a day, far less than the hours lost to the paper book, and in line with what small shops already pay for billing apps.

The price comes from one shop's answer and the idea hasn't been tested beyond that, but they told me they would use it.

Code

arkia09 / Ledgerly

Ledgerly

Photograph a page of a paper credit ledger. A local Gemma model (via Ollama) reads it, you correct mistakes, and the app reports who owes what and for how long.

Layout

  • extraction/ Step 1: model prompt, schema, single/batch runners, scoring
  • backend/ Step 2: Django API (SQLite, no login)
  • frontend/ Step 3: React + TypeScript app (Vite)
  • finetune/ Optional: fine-tune a vision model on Tinker and compare with the baseline (see its README)
  • data/pages/ test photos (gitignored: may contain customer data)
  • data/ground_truth/ your hand-written correct answers, one JSON per photo
  • data/outputs/ model outputs per run (gitignored)

Setup (Windows PowerShell)

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
ollama pull gemma4:e4b

Step 1 workflow

  1. Put photos in data/pages/ (page01.jpg, page02.jpg, ...).
  2. For each, copy data/ground_truth/_template.json to page01.json and fill in the true rows Set "page_type" to neat, messy or mixed.
  3. Edit the layout line in extraction/prompt.txt to match your ledger.
  4. …
View on GitHub

Django + SQLite backend, React + TypeScript frontend, and an extraction/ft/ folder that holds the whole fine-tuning pipeline: dataset.py, train.py, sampler.py, evaluate.py, compare.py.

How I Built It 

photo ──▶ preprocess
      ──▶ vision model ──▶ JSON { rows: [ {date, name, item, amount, type, struck_out} ] }
      ──▶ pydantic schema check
      ──▶ review screen (you fix rows) ──▶ confirm ──▶ ledger + aging report
                                                │
                    corrections ◀───────────────┘  (next training run, --from-db)

Each row has exactly six fields. type is credit (udhar) or payment (jama), and struck_out is true when the shopkeeper has crossed a row out, so it is stored but not counted:

{ "date": "15/10", "name": "Ramesh Kumar", "item": "Atta (5 kg)",
  "amount": 240, "type": "credit", "struck_out": false }

Step 1: the baseline, with a local Gemma

The first version ran Gemma 4 e4b locally through Ollama. Nothing leaves the computer, which matters for a book full of customers' names and debts. It works, but it takes about 159 seconds per page on my CPU.

Step 2: the data (the boring part that decides everything)

I labelled 14 pages by hand (took me 2 hours), one JSON of ground truth per photo. Then I split them so the model is judged on pages it has never seen:

  • Held out (5 pages, 50 rows): page02, page04, page06 (my original neat, messy and mixed pages) plus page09 and page10.
  • Trained on (9 pages): the rest.

I picked page09 and page10 as test pages on purpose. Several of my new pages repeat each other's customers and amounts (page 8 and page 14 are nearly identical). If a test page has a twin in training, the score is inflated. Those two had no twins.

Nine pages is tiny, so dataset.py adds three augmented copies of each page (small rotation, brightness, contrast and crop). That makes 36 training examples, 79,764 tokens per epoch.

Step 3: fine-tuning on Tinker

Choosing the model

The input is a photograph, so I needed a vision model. My first choice, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, died on the first real run with 400: base_model ... is not supported. The public docs still listed it. So I asked the server what my key could use (ServiceClient().get_server_capabilities()), and the list had moved on to Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6, plus Nemotron and others.

I picked Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: a mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active parameters, which keeps training and sampling cheap, in the same size class as the model I'd planned. A free --dry-run rendered every example with the real tokenizer and image processor before I spent anything, and the renderer it chose (qwen3_5) matched what tinker_cookbook recommends for that model.

I used Tinker to LoRA fine-tune it with the settings in train.py:

Setting Value
Method LoRA, rank 16
Epochs / batch size 4 / 4, so 36 steps
Learning rate 1e-4, decaying to 1e-5
Renderer qwen3_5 (matches get_recommended_renderer_name)
Training cost about $0.38 of credit ($10.00 to $9.62)

Every example is a (photo, correct JSON) pair.

epoch 1/4 step 1/36  loss/token 0.1466
epoch 1/4 step 9/36  loss/token 0.0185
epoch 2/4 step 18/36 loss/token 0.0050
epoch 3/4 step 27/36 loss/token 0.0013
epoch 4/4 step 36/36 loss/token 0.0008

I'm not treating that curve as a result. It's loss on training pages the model saw four times each, so it says the run was healthy, not that the model is good.

Step 4: the evaluation

ft/evaluate.py runs the untouched base model and the fine-tuned model on the five held-out pages and scores both with my own score.py. Each true row has to be matched to a predicted row, and then name, amount, date, type and crossed-out flag are checked. A row counts as "full" only when all five are right.

The base model scored 0%. I want to be precise about why. It did not read the pages badly. On all five pages it failed to produce valid JSON for my schema (wrong shape, no JSON object at all, or text after the JSON). score.py can only score what it can parse, so every page became "found 0 rows". That number measures instruction-following on one schema, not handwriting, so I'm not using it as my "before". Gemma is my baseline, because it produces valid output.

Fine-tuned Qwen against local Gemma, 50 rows, same pages, same checker:

Gemma 4 e4b (local) Qwen3.6 fine-tuned (Tinker)
Full row correct 41/50 (82%) 44/50 (88%)
Name 46/50 45/50
Amount 48/50 49/50
Date 47/50 49/50
Type (credit vs payment) 44/50 (88%) 49/50 (98%)
Crossed out 47/50 48/50
Extra rows invented 0 0
Seconds per page 159 s (laptop CPU) 12 s (Tinker cloud GPU)

Fully right rows by kind of page (this is the part I'd look at before trusting any single percentage):

Page type Rows Gemma 4 e4b (local) Qwen3.6 fine-tuned
Neat (page02, page09, page10) 30 26 (87%) 28 (93%)
Messy (page04) 10 7 (70%) 10 (100%)
Mixed Hindi/English (page06) 10 8 (80%) 6 (60%)

What stands out:

  1. Credit versus payment went from 88% to 98%. In a ledger that is the field that matters most: mixing up udhar and jama flips the sign on someone's balance.
  2. Three more rows fully right out of 50 (82% to 88%), with dates, amounts and crossed-out flags all a little better and no invented rows.
  3. 12 seconds a page instead of 159. That compares a cloud GPU with my laptop CPU, so read it as "hosted versus on my machine", not as a model-size result.
  4. Where it's level or behind: names (45 against Gemma's 46) and my one mixed Hindi/English page (6 of 10 rows against 8). On the neat and messy pages it got 28 of 30 and 10 of 10 rows fully right.

With 50 test rows, a one or two row gap is noise, so I trust the type and speed results most.

Two details from walking through every row in compare.html:

  • One label was my mistake. On page06, row 7, my ground-truth JSON said the row was crossed out, but I never crossed it out on the paper. Both models said "not crossed out", so both were marked wrong for being right. I corrected that one label after seeing the results and rescored both models, so the numbers above include the fix.
  • One real miss: the fine-tuned model wrote "Pooja" in Latin letters where the ledger has the name in Devanagari. It's the same person, but the tool is meant to copy what's written, so I left it counted as wrong. Several of the other name misses were rows Gemma read correctly.

Step 5: seeing the mistakes, not just the percentages

ft/compare.py builds one HTML page: my photo, my ground truth, and every model side by side, with wrong fields in red and the correct value underneath. I used it to find that the mixed page was where the fine-tuned model lost rows.

Using it in the app

One environment variable decides who reads the page:

$env:LEDGERLY_EXTRACTOR = "tinker"   # default is the local Gemma via Ollama

The default keeps every photo on the computer. With tinker, each photo is sent to Tinker's cloud to be read by the fine-tuned model, and the README says so. The API key lives in an environment variable and nowhere in the repo.

What I got wrong on the way

  • I almost trained on three pages. I had put all eight new pages into the held-out list. That left the training set exactly where it started. Reading the dry-run's "36 examples" line is what caught the mistake.

  • My new photos were .jpeg, and the pipeline looked for .jpg. They were skipped without a single warning. Renaming fixed it.

    What I learned

  • Label quality matters as much as quantity. Some of the mistakes I found in compare.html were mine, not the model's: a "crossed out" label on a row I never crossed out. A model can only be as consistent as the labels it is trained and judged on.

  • Measure the baseline fairly. Base Qwen's 0% looked dramatic and meant "can't follow my JSON format". Gemma was the honest comparison.

  • Look at the rows, not just the percentages. The scoreboard said the fine-tuned model was a little better. The side-by-side page showed where: credit versus payment and the neat and messy pages, not the mixed one.

  • Dry-run first. The whole fine-tune cost about forty cents because I rendered everything for free before spending any credit.

What's next

  • Learn the neighbours' khata. Label a few pages in their layout and run the same pipeline. Every page they confirm in the app becomes training data (--from-db).
  • More writers. My own handwriting is in all 14 pages. Pages from other hands will show how far the model carries.
  • Publish the adapter on Hugging Face (Tinker can push a checkpoint straight there), so anyone can run it on their own hardware.
  • Package it as an app so a shopkeeper can use it without a laptop.

The review screen is part of the design: the model proposes the rows, the shopkeeper confirms them, and nothing reaches the ledger unchecked.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • It stays on the shopkeeper's computer. A khata is a list of who owes whom. With open weights the default path never uploads a photo, and the cloud path is opt-in and said out loud.
  • I could change the model and measure it. Tinker let me fine-tune open weights for about 38 cents, and I could run that against an open baseline on the same pages with the same scorer. Swapping the base model is one variable (TINKER_BASE_MODEL).
  • I could see why it was wrong. The comparison page shows each wrong field next to the right value, so I could tell a reading error from a spelling variant instead of trusting one score.

  • The result is reproducible. Open weights, my labelled pages, my scorer and the saved outputs are all in the repo, so anyone can rerun the comparison.

    Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Tinker: LoRA fine-tune of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 36 augmented examples, scored on 5 held-out pages against a local baseline, for about $0.38.

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 e4b runs locally through Ollama as the private default and as the baseline the fine-tuned model has to beat.

Built with Claude and tea ☕.

articles.title: Nuxt 4.6 useSession: Server Sessions Without a Database
articles.description: Nuxt 4.6 ships useSession and runtimeConfig.appSecret — real, sealed-cookie sessions with no database or session store. How it works, plus a cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
You build a login endpoint. It checks the password, and now you need to remember that this particular visitor is logged in the next time their browser shows up — which, on a server, is a completely new, unrelated request. Reach for useState and it resets every time, because it only lives for one server render. Reach for a module-scope variable and you've just reintroduced the cross-request leak this series already covered. So you either stand up a database table for sessions, or reach for a third-party module to seal a cookie for you.

As of Nuxt 4.6, released October 5, 2026, you don't need either. Nuxt core now ships useSession, a server session that lives entirely inside a tamper-proof cookie — no session store, no database row, no Redis.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why useState and a module-scope variable both fail to "remember" a visitor across real, separate requests
  • Set runtimeConfig.appSecret and understand what it's actually for
  • Use useSession to read, update, and clear session data from a server route
  • Explain why a sealed cookie is safe to trust — what happens when someone edits it
  • Avoid the one import mistake (NUXT_E8012) that trips people up migrating to nuxt/server

Who this is for

You've read or can follow the useState vs ref episode — or at least you accept its conclusion: Nuxt's server has no memory of its own between requests unless you give it one on purpose. This article is about the tool Nuxt 4.6 gives you for that: a cookie-backed session. No prior auth-library experience needed.

This article is written against Nuxt 4.6 (verified against the nuxt package's GitHub releases and npm dist-tags on October 17, 2026 — 4.6.0 shipped October 5, with patch releases 4.6.1 and 4.6.2 following; neither patch touches session handling, so everything below applies unchanged across all three). Code uses the Nuxt 4 app/ directory convention; server/ stays at the project root either way, same as every other episode in this series.

Table of contents

  • The problem: nothing the server does survives the request
  • The mental model: stateless server, stateful cookie
  • Building it, stage by stage
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices: useSession vs useState vs a database
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet

The problem: nothing the server does survives the request

Here's a login handler that looks reasonable:

// server/api/login.post.ts
import { defineEventHandler, readBody } from 'nuxt/server'

let currentUser: { id: number; name: string } | null = null // wrong — see below

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const { username, password } = await readBody(event)
  const user = await verifyCredentials(username, password)
  currentUser = user // "remember" them... where, exactly?
  return { ok: true }
})

// server/api/me.get.ts
import { defineEventHandler } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler(() => {
  return { user: currentUser } // undefined for the next visitor, or worse
})

This is the same bug the useState episode walked through: currentUser is a module-scope variable, created once when the server process starts, shared by every request that process ever handles. In development, with one tab open, it looks like it works — you log in, you call /api/me, you get your user back. In production, with concurrent traffic, a second visitor's request can run between the two and overwrite currentUser before you read it. You'd see someone else's session, or a login that silently "loses" itself under load.

The instinct to fix this with useState doesn't work either, for a different reason: useState isolates data within a single server-side render — it exists to get data safely into the SSR payload for one request's Vue app instance, and that instance is thrown away the moment the response is sent. It was never meant to persist between two separate HTTP requests made minutes apart; it isn't that kind of tool, and calling it from server/ doesn't even work (there's no Vue app instance there — that's the Nitro server routes episode's subject).

What you actually need is something that survives between requests without living in server memory at all — because the server might restart, and in production it's rarely a single process.

The mental model: stateless server, stateful cookie

The mental model: a Nitro request handler, by itself, is stateless — it has no memory of any earlier request, by design. The only way information crosses from one request to the next is if the client carries it back: either a reference (a session ID the server looks up in a database) or the data itself, sealed so the client can carry it without being able to read or forge it.

useSession, new in Nuxt 4.6 via the nuxt/server import source, is the second approach. When you call it, Nuxt:

  1. reads the session cookie on the incoming request, if one exists;
  2. unseals it — decrypts it and verifies it hasn't been tampered with, using a key derived from your app's secret;
  3. hands you a session.data object to read and a session.update() to change it;
  4. on update(), reseals the (possibly new) data into a fresh cookie and attaches it to the response.

Nothing is stored on the server. The cookie is the session. That's also why it needs a secret: without one, anyone could write their own cookie and hand your server whatever session data they wanted.

A term of art: "sealing" here means authenticated encryption — the data is both encrypted (unreadable without the key) and signed (any edit invalidates it). Nuxt's session helpers use the iron sealing format via h3, the same primitive underneath, so a one-character edit to the cookie doesn't produce different session data — it just fails to unseal at all, and the request is treated as having no session.

Building it, stage by stage

Stage 1 — the one secret your whole app needs

Nuxt 4.6 introduces a single root secret: runtimeConfig.appSecret, set via the NUXT_APP_SECRET environment variable. Session sealing, and any future module that needs a secret, derives its own purpose-specific key from it internally — you configure one value, not a different secret per feature.

# generate one, once, per environment
openssl rand -base64 32

# .env (never commit this)
NUXT_APP_SECRET=the-output-of-the-command-above

Key concept: in local development, if you haven't set one, Nuxt generates and saves a secret for you automatically and warns the first time something derives a key from it. That convenience is dev-only — a production build never auto-generates a secret. If you deploy without setting NUXT_APP_SECRET, you're deploying without one, not getting a free one; treat it the same as any other missing required credential, and set it before your first production deploy, not after something breaks.

Stage 2 — reading and writing session data 

// server/api/visit.get.ts
import { defineEventHandler, useSession } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const session = await useSession<{ visits: number }>(event)

  await session.update({ visits: (session.data.visits ?? 0) + 1 })

  return { visits: session.data.visits }
})

Call /api/visit once and you get { "visits": 1 }. Refresh and it climbs: 2, 3, 4 — across completely separate requests, with no database anywhere in this code. Open the same route in a different browser (no shared cookie) and it starts at 1 again, independently. That's the whole point: the state travels with the visitor, sealed into their own cookie, not with the server process.

Key concept: unlike using h3's session utility directly — where you must pass a password of at least 32 characters yourself — Nuxt's wrapper derives that password from runtimeConfig.appSecret for you. appSecret really is the only secret you manage.

Stage 3 — logging someone in, and out 

// server/api/login.post.ts
import { defineEventHandler, readBody, useSession } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const { username, password } = await readBody<{ username: string; password: string }>(event)
  const user = await verifyCredentials(username, password) // your own check

  const session = await useSession<{ userId: number }>(event)
  await session.update({ userId: user.id })

  return { ok: true }
})

// server/api/logout.post.ts
import { defineEventHandler, useSession } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const session = await useSession(event)
  await session.clear() // removes the session data AND the cookie
  return { ok: true }
})

Every later request that carries the resulting cookie can call useSession(event) again and read session.data.userId straight back — no lookup, no round trip to anywhere.

Stage 4 — the migration trap: NUXT_E8012

nuxt/server is a new, parallel import source alongside the classic auto-imported server/ utilities (which come from h3 under the hood either way). They are not meant to be mixed in the same handler:

// ❌ mixes an auto-imported helper with an explicit nuxt/server import
import { useSession } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => { // defineEventHandler here is auto-imported, not explicit
  const session = await useSession(event)
  // …
})

Doing this throws NUXT_E8012 at build or runtime, depending on what's mixed. The fix is mechanical: once a handler touches nuxt/server, import everything it uses — defineEventHandler, readBody, useSession, whatever else — from nuxt/server explicitly, as every example above does. Nothing requires you to migrate existing handlers that only use the classic auto-imports; the rule only bites when you start mixing the two styles in the same file.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • The cookie has a size limit, because it's a cookie. A database-backed session can hold anything; a sealed-cookie session is bounded by how much a browser will send back in a header (a few KB, practically). Keep session.data small — an ID, a role, a couple of flags — not a shopping cart's full contents.
  • It isn't reachable from a Vue component. useSession lives in nuxt/server, for server routes and middleware only. To get session-derived data into a page, expose it from an endpoint and read it with useFetch/useAsyncData — the same request/dedupe rules from the useAsyncData episode apply.
  • Rotating appSecret logs everyone out at once. Every existing cookie was sealed with keys derived from the old secret; once the secret changes, every one of them fails to unseal and is treated as "no session." That's correct behavior, not a bug — but plan rotations knowing the blast radius.
  • This scales horizontally for free. Because there's no server-side store, any number of server instances can validate the same session as long as they share the same appSecret — no shared Redis, no sticky sessions, nothing to keep in sync.
  • maxAge and idleTimeout are separate knobs. maxAge is an absolute lifetime from creation; idleTimeout is a sliding window measured from the last request that touched the session. Set at least maxAge explicitly — don't rely on defaults you haven't checked for your use case.

Best practices: useSession vs useState vs a database

You need… Reach for
Data to reach the client within this render's payload, safely per-request useState
A small, server-only fact that must survive across separate requests from the same visitor (login status, a role, a cart ID) useSession
Data too large for a cookie, shared across devices, or queryable/auditable on its own A real database, keyed by a session ID
A value every request needs and that never changes per-visitor runtimeConfig, not a session at all

Never put secrets inside session data expecting them to stay hidden from the visitor who owns that session — sealing hides the data from everyone else, not from the person whose cookie it is. And never reach for a module-scope variable to "remember" anything about a specific visitor; that bug is exactly what this series' useState vs ref episode walked through.

FAQ

Is Nuxt's useSession the same as h3's useSession?

It's built on the same underlying session and sealing mechanism from h3, exposed through the new nuxt/server import source so it's portable across Nitro v2, Nitro v3, and the experimental Vite-based server Nuxt is also building. The difference that matters day to day is that Nuxt fills in the password for you from runtimeConfig.appSecret.

Do I still need a module like nuxt-auth-utils?

For the cookie-sealing mechanism itself, no — that's now in Nuxt core. A full auth module still earns its keep for things core doesn't do: OAuth provider flows, refresh-token rotation, pre-built login UI. Read what a module adds on top before assuming you still need it for sessions alone.

What happens if I forget to set NUXT_APP_SECRET in production?

Nothing generates one for you — that only happens in local development. Treat a missing appSecret the same as any other missing required environment variable: set it before your first deploy, store it the way you store any other secret, and never commit it.

Can a visitor edit their own session cookie to grant themselves more access?

No, as long as sealing is doing its job: editing even one character of a sealed cookie breaks the seal, and useSession treats an unsealable cookie as no session at all — not as the edited data. They can delete their session or get logged out; they can't forge a different one without your appSecret.

Does this replace a database for user accounts?

No. useSession holds the small, ephemeral fact that a particular request belongs to a particular already-authenticated visitor. The accounts themselves — usernames, hashed passwords, profile data — still belong in a real datastore; the session just carries a reference to one, such as a user ID.

Cheat sheet 

// 1. One secret, once per environment
// .env → NUXT_APP_SECRET=<openssl rand -base64 32>
// (dev: auto-generated if missing. prod builds: never auto-generated — you must set it.)

// 2. Always import everything from nuxt/server once you touch it (avoids NUXT_E8012)
import { defineEventHandler, readBody, useSession } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  // 3. Read + create
  const session = await useSession<{ userId?: number; visits?: number }>(event)

  // 4. Update (reseals the cookie automatically)
  await session.update({ visits: (session.data.visits ?? 0) + 1 })

  // 5. Read back
  const current = session.data

  // 6. Log out / destroy
  // await session.clear()

  return current
})
Task Do this Notes
Set the one required secret NUXT_APP_SECRET env var Dev auto-generates one; prod never does
Read session data const s = await useSession(event) → s.data Returns {} if none exists yet
Change session data await s.update({ key: value }) Merges and reseals the cookie
End the session await s.clear() Removes data and the cookie
Reach it from a Vue component Expose it from an endpoint, call with useFetch useSession is server-only
Avoid NUXT_E8012 Import everything in that handler from nuxt/server Don't mix with classic auto-imports

Key takeaways

  • A Nitro request handler has no memory between requests on its own — that's the same lesson as the cross-request state leak, applied constructively this time.
  • Nuxt 4.6's useSession, from nuxt/server, seals session data into the cookie itself: no database, no Redis, and it scales across instances for free.
  • runtimeConfig.appSecret (NUXT_APP_SECRET) is the one secret everything derives from — set it yourself before deploying; Nuxt only auto-generates one in development.
  • Sealing means tampering breaks the cookie instead of forging new data — that's why it's safe to trust.
  • useSession and useState solve different problems: one survives across real requests, the other gets data into a single render's payload. Mixing them up is the bug.

articles.title: PHP 8.6 Adds foo(?, 2) Partial Application. Here's How to Write It in TypeScript
articles.description: PHP 8.6's ? and ... placeholders mapped to TypeScript: arrow closures, bind() and its limits, and a typed partial() built on variadic tuples.
articles.body_html:
• Book: PHP to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The PHP 8.5 release page shows off the new pipe operator with this chain:

$slug = $title
    |> trim(...)
    |> (fn($str) => str_replace(' ', '-', $str))
    |> (fn($str) => str_replace('.', '', $str))
    |> strtolower(...);

Two of those four steps are arrow functions whose only job is to move $str into the third slot of str_replace(). In PHP 8.6 each one shrinks to str_replace(' ', '-', ?). The Partial Function Application v2 RFC by Larry Garfield and Arnaud Le Blanc closed its vote on December 5, 2025, adopted 33-0-0, targeting PHP 8.6. That release is already in release candidates, so its feature set is frozen: the php.net archive shows RC3 out on October 8.

If you write PHP by day and TypeScript the rest of the time, the next question is what the same move looks like on the other side. There are three answers, and each one gives up something PHP's version keeps.

What ? and ... do in PHP 8.6

A call with at least one placeholder doesn't run the function. It returns a Closure. ? stands for exactly one argument. ... stands for zero or more and can appear once, at the end. Positional values and ? come first, named arguments after. The closure copies the real function's parameter types, names and return type.

function fee(int $cents, float $rate, string $currency): string
{
    return sprintf('%.2f %s', $cents * $rate / 100, $currency);
}

$eur    = fee(?, 0.029, 'EUR');         // fn(int $cents)
$at1999 = fee(1999, ?, 'EUR');          // fn(float $rate)
$tail   = fee(1999, ...);               // fn(float, string)
$thunk  = fee(1999, 0.029, 'EUR', ...); // fn(): string

// Named placeholders: the closure takes (currency, cents)
$byName = fee(currency: ?, cents: ?, rate: 0.029);

echo $eur(1999); // 0.58 EUR

Two details matter for the TypeScript side. First, bound arguments are evaluated when the partial is created, not when it's called. The RFC contrasts the two forms with an example of this shape:

// currentRate() runs once, right here
$partial = fee(?, currentRate(), 'EUR');

// currentRate() runs on every call
$arrow = fn(int $c) => fee($c, currentRate(), 'EUR');

Second, a follow-up RFC on optional parameters, accepted 25-0 with one abstention in May 2026, makes every parameter created by ? required, even when the original had a default. Parameters pulled in by ... keep their optionality.

The arrow function is the TypeScript default

TypeScript has no placeholder syntax, so the everyday answer is the thing PHP 8.6 replaces: a closure that forwards.

function fee(cents: number, rate: number, currency: string) {
  return `${((cents * rate) / 100).toFixed(2)} ${currency}`;
}

const eurFee = (cents: number) => fee(cents, 0.029, "EUR");
const rateFor1999 = (rate: number) => fee(1999, rate, "EUR");
const thunkFee = () => fee(1999, 0.029, "EUR");

console.log(eurFee(1999)); // 0.58 EUR

It covers every PHP form: a hole at the front, a hole in the middle, a zero-argument thunk. What it costs is repetition. You restate each open parameter's type by hand, and if fee changes its signature, the wrapper's annotation is one more place to update.

It also evaluates lazily, like PHP's arrow form and unlike fee(?, ...). There's one more difference a PHP developer will trip on: PHP arrow functions capture outer variables by value when they're created, while a JavaScript closure reads the variable itself, so it sees every later reassignment.

bind() only fills the front

The built-in alternative is Function.prototype.bind. Since TypeScript 3.2, the strictBindCallApply option (part of strict) types it properly instead of returning any.

const forCents = fee.bind(null, 1999);
// takes (rate, currency), returns string

console.log(forCents(0.029, "EUR")); // 0.58 EUR

The typing comes from CallableFunction in the lib.es5.d.ts declarations, where bind is declared over a function with parameters [...A, ...B]: A is what you pass, B is what's left. That gets you PHP's fee(1999, ...) with correct types.

It stops there. bind only fills arguments from the left, so fee(?, 0.029, 'EUR') has no bind equivalent. You always pass a this value, even for a plain function. And the 3.2 release notes named two limits at launch: generic functions lost their type parameters, and for an overloaded function only the last overload is modeled.

A typed partial() with a placeholder

You can get the middle-of-the-list hole back with a placeholder value and some type-level work. Lodash's _.partial accepts _ as a placeholder; what follows is a small typed version built on the variadic tuple types TypeScript 4.0 introduced and the conditional-type infer keyword that has been around since TypeScript 2.8.

Save this as partial.ts:

export {};

const _ = Symbol("placeholder");
type _ = typeof _;

type Arr = readonly unknown[];

// Each argument is either a real value or the placeholder.
type Slots<P extends Arr> = { [K in keyof P]: P[K] | _ };

// Walk params and args together; keep params that got a _.
type Holes<P extends Arr, A extends Arr> =
  A extends readonly [infer AH, ...infer AT]
    ? P extends readonly [infer PH, ...infer PT]
      ? AH extends _
        ? [PH, ...Holes<PT, AT>]
        : Holes<PT, AT>
      : []
    : P;

function partial<P extends Arr, R, A extends Slots<P>>(
  f: (...args: P) => R,
  ...args: A
): (...rest: Holes<P, A>) => R;
function partial(f: (...a: any[]) => any, ...args: any[]) {
  return (...rest: any[]) => {
    let i = 0;
    const full = args.map((a) => (a === _ ? rest[i++] : a));
    return f(...full, ...rest.slice(i));
  };
}

function fee(cents: number, rate: number, currency: string) {
  return `${((cents * rate) / 100).toFixed(2)} ${currency}`;
}

const eur = partial(fee, _, 0.029, "EUR");   // (cents) => string
const at1999 = partial(fee, 1999, _, "EUR"); // (rate) => string
const twoHoles = partial(fee, _, 0.029, _);  // (cents, currency)

console.log(eur(1999));              // 0.58 EUR
console.log(at1999(0.035));          // 0.70 EUR
console.log(twoHoles(10000, "USD")); // 2.90 USD

// partial(fee, _, "0.029", "EUR"); // type error: not a number
// partial(fee, _, 0.029);          // type error: 3 slots needed

Slots<P> is a mapped type over the parameter tuple, so every position accepts its real type or _. Because A must fit all of Slots<P>, leaving a slot out is a compile error, which matches PHP throwing ArgumentCountError for a ?-only call that doesn't cover the required parameters. Holes<P, A> walks both tuples one element at a time with infer and keeps the parameter types that sat under a _. That tuple becomes the rest parameter of the returned function.

The implementation signature uses any on purpose. The public overload carries the types; the body only swaps placeholders for incoming arguments in order and appends anything extra.

PHP's fee(1999, ...) form doesn't need a placeholder at all. The partialCall example from the TypeScript 4.0 notes already covers it, and with every argument supplied it gives you a thunk:

function partialHead<H extends Arr, T extends Arr, R>(
  f: (...args: [...H, ...T]) => R,
  ...head: H
): (...tail: T) => R {
  return (...tail: T) => f(...head, ...tail);
}

const later = partialHead(fee, 1999, 0.029, "EUR"); // () => string
console.log(later()); // 0.58 EUR

Both helpers evaluate bound arguments at creation time, like PHP. Append this to the file to see the difference from a closure:

let rate = 0.029;
const bound = partial(fee, _, rate, "EUR");
const live = (cents: number) => fee(cents, rate, "EUR");
rate = 0.05;

console.log(bound(10000)); // 2.90 EUR: rate read at creation
console.log(live(10000));  // 5.00 EUR: rate read at call time

Run it with tsx:

npx tsx partial.ts
npx -p typescript tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2022 partial.ts

The second command matters. tsx strips types and runs the file, and its docs say plainly that it does not type-check your code. The two commented-out bad calls only fail under tsc.

Where PHP's version still wins

Named arguments. fee(currency: ?, cents: ?, rate: 0.029) works on the original function. TypeScript has no named arguments, so the closest you get is an options object and a helper that fixes some keys:

type FeeArgs = { cents: number; rate: number; currency: string };

const feeOf = ({ cents, rate, currency }: FeeArgs) =>
  fee(cents, rate, currency);

function fix<O extends object, K extends keyof O, R>(
  f: (opts: O) => R,
  fixed: Pick<O, K>,
): (rest: Omit<O, K>) => R {
  return (rest) => f({ ...fixed, ...rest } as O);
}

const usd = fix(feeOf, { currency: "USD" });
console.log(usd({ cents: 10000, rate: 0.029 })); // 2.90 USD

It works, but you had to change the function's shape to get there, and the as O cast is there because the compiler can't prove that Pick<O, K> plus Omit<O, K> adds back up to O.

Signature fidelity. PHP's closure copies names, types and by-reference parameters from the real function (defaults too, for parameters pulled in by ...), and named placeholders can reorder them. The Holes tuple keeps types but not parameter names, so editor hints get vaguer than the original.

Overloads and this. When TypeScript infers from an overloaded function, the handbook says inferences come from the last signature, and that applies to partial() as much as to bind. The helper also drops this, while the RFC lets you partially apply methods, static methods and invokable objects directly.

Syntax. In PHP, ? is part of the language, and the RFC says the compiler turns some pipe forms such as foo(?) into direct calls. In TypeScript, every partial() is a runtime closure plus an array walk.

TypeScript's advantage is the compile-time check: the two commented-out calls at the bottom of partial.ts show up red in your editor before anything runs.

For most code, the arrow function is still the right TypeScript answer. It's one line, and there's nothing to explain in review. Reach for partial() when you're building callbacks in a loop or feeding a pipeline and the hole sits in the middle of the argument list.

If this was useful

This post is one feature mapped across two languages, with the places where the mapping leaks. That's what PHP to TypeScript does for a whole PHP 8+ habit set: sync-to-async, generics and discriminated unions. It's part of The TypeScript Library:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

If you came here from PHP, PHP to TypeScript stands in for the first book, and The TypeScript Type System is where Slots and Holes stop looking like magic. Shipping TypeScript at work already? Add TypeScript in Production. The whole set is at xgabriel.com/the-typescript-library.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Why CAGR Is Not the Same as Your Actual Year-by-Year Return
articles.description: CAGR is useful because it compresses a beginning value, ending value, and time span into one...
articles.body_html:
CAGR is useful because it compresses a beginning value, ending value, and time span into one annualized rate. It is also easy to misuse as if an investment grew at that rate every year. I built the calculator to show both the compact percentage and a reconstructed year-by-year path, making that distinction hard to miss.

The core formula describes an equivalent rate

The computed result normalizes the inputs and clamps the number of years:

const b = Number(beginValue.value) || 0;
const e = Number(endValue.value) || 0;
const Y = Math.min(
  Math.max(Math.floor(Number(years.value) || 0), 1),
  80
);
if (b <= 0 || e <= 0) return null;

const cagr = Math.pow(e / b, 1 / Y) - 1;

The formula asks: “What constant annual rate would turn the beginning value into the ending value over Y years?” It does not inspect the path between those endpoints. A portfolio could crash and recover and still have the same CAGR as a smooth line.

Total return answers a different question

The source keeps simple growth separate:

const totalReturn = e / b - 1;
const gain = e - b;

totalReturn is the complete change across the period. cagr is that change annualized with compounding. A 21 percent total return over three years is not a 21 percent annual return; the equivalent annual rate is smaller. Showing both prevents a familiar percentage from being read with the wrong time unit.

The yearly table is a reconstructed path

Once CAGR is known, the tool builds illustrative values:

const rows = [];
for (let y = 0; y <= Y; y++) {
  const value = b * Math.pow(1 + cagr, y);
  rows.push({
    year: y,
    value,
    growth: value - b,
  });
}

This table is not historical data. It is the smooth path implied by the equivalent rate. That makes it useful for explaining compounding, but it should not be mistaken for the actual annual returns that produced the endpoint.

The formatter makes the sign explicit:

function fmtPct(val) {
  if (val === null || val === undefined || isNaN(val)) return "—";
  const pct = val * 100;
  const sign = pct > 0 ? "+" : "";
  return `${sign}${pct.toFixed(2)}%`;
}

Negative CAGR is valid when the ending value is lower, while zero gets no plus sign. The input guard rejects zero or negative endpoints because the logarithmic intuition behind growth rates becomes misleading for this simple ratio model.

The major limitation is what the formula leaves out: deposits, withdrawals, dividends, taxes, fees, inflation, volatility, and cash-flow timing. If money enters or leaves during the period, a money-weighted or time-weighted return measure may be more appropriate. The 80-year cap is also a display boundary, not a statement about finance.

A smooth chart can be honest if it labels the assumption

The reconstructed rows start at year zero, where value equals the beginning value and growth is zero. Each later row compounds the same equivalent rate again. That makes the table a teaching aid: it shows what “annualized” means without claiming that the account actually followed that line.

There is also a useful relationship to check manually. The final row should equal the ending input apart from floating-point and display rounding, because the rate was derived from that endpoint. gain should equal end - begin, while the cumulative growth in the last row should express the same difference. These simple invariants are valuable when changing a financial component; they catch swapped endpoints and off-by-one year loops quickly.

Negative results deserve the same care as positive ones. If the ending value is lower, fmtPct adds no plus sign and the reconstructed path declines each year. That path is still only an equivalent path. A real investment can have negative years followed by recovery, and CAGR alone cannot tell the story of volatility or drawdown.

If a future version adds cash flows, I would not quietly overload these inputs. I would introduce a separate return method and explain its assumptions, because a single “CAGR” label should not start pretending to be an internal rate of return calculator.

The formatter rounds currency-like values to whole units while leaving the percentage at two decimal places. That is a display choice, not a loss of precision in the calculation. Keeping raw numeric fields in the returned result means another presentation—more decimals, a chart tooltip, or a localized currency symbol—can be added without rewriting the formula.

That split between raw result and formatted text is especially helpful when comparing two scenarios: the UI can show friendly numbers while tests still inspect the unrounded cagr, gain, and row values.

The final result remains a model, not a guarantee, and the input values still need context before anyone makes a decision.

I would also avoid comparing CAGR values with different time windows as if they were automatically equivalent. The exponent normalizes each result to an annual rate, but a two-year result and a twenty-year result can have very different uncertainty, volatility, and practical meaning. The component can calculate both because the formula is compact; interpretation still belongs to the person supplying the beginning and ending values.

That boundary is useful for implementation too. The view does not fetch market prices, infer missing dates, or decorate the result with a prediction. It receives three numbers, calculates a reproducible equivalent rate, and exposes the intermediate rows. Fewer hidden inputs make the output easier to audit, even when the financial story behind those inputs is complicated.

I turned this explanation into a small free tool: CAGR Calculator.

articles.title: Hijack Radar: your lockfile said you were safe. Your dependency graph knew better.
articles.description: Monday, September 8, 2025   A maintainer of some of the most-used packages on npm gets an...
articles.body_html:
Monday, September 8, 2025

A maintainer of some of the most-used packages on npm gets an email. It says their two-factor settings need updating before the 10th. The link looks like npm. It isn't.

Minutes later, new versions of 18 packages appear on the registry, chalk and debug among them. Together they're downloaded about 2.6 billion times a week. The new code quietly rewrites crypto wallet transactions in the browser. The bad versions are pulled within hours, but every engineering team spends that afternoon asking the same question:

Were we hit?

The obvious way to answer is to search your repos for debug in package.json. We did exactly that across 17 real open-source codebases: VS Code, Playwright, Bitwarden, Jitsi Meet, Expensify and more.

One repo declares debug. All seventeen install it.

The other sixteen pull it in through chains like vscode → eslint@10.8.0 → debug@4.4.3. A text search can't see those chains. A graph can. That gap is the whole project.

What Hijack Radar does

Hijack Radar is an AI agent for the attacks CVE scanners weren't built for: account takeovers and hijacked releases. You ask in plain English, and it answers from a FalkorDB graph of what your repos really install, with the exact path behind every answer.

  • "If the npm account qix were phished, what would it reach?" That account publishes 7 packages, and they reach all 17 repos. The answer comes back in milliseconds, with a path for each repo.
  • "MAL-2025-46974 just dropped. Are we affected?" This is the real advisory from that day. A lockfile scanner says safe, because no lockfile pins debug@4.4.2. The agent says that honestly, then checks the version ranges: 217 of them accept the hijacked release, so your next npm update would have pulled it into every repo.
  • "Where is our next xz?" PageRank over the dependency graph, filtered to packages that a single npm account controls. These are the load-bearing packages nobody is watching.
  • "We'll pin debug with overrides everywhere. Remember that, and draft an issue for jitsi-meet." The decision is stored as a dated node in the graph, and the agent drafts the fix for the owning team.

Every answer sits next to an evidence panel: the tool calls it made, how long FalkorDB took, and a graph of every dependency path it found, with repos in blue and the compromised package in red. There's also a radar view: the 17 repos as dots, one ring per dependency hop. Replay an attack and the sweep lights up every exposed repo on the ring where the graph reaches it.

Why this has to be a graph

Supply-chain questions are questions about connections, and they're several hops deep:

(:Maintainer)-[:MAINTAINS]->(:Package)-[:HAS_VERSION]->(:Version)
(:Repo)-[:DEPENDS_ON {range}]->(:Version)-[:DEPENDS_ON {range}]->(:Version)
(:Advisory)-[:AFFECTS]->(:Version)
(:Team)-[:OWNS]->(:Repo)
(:Decision)-[:ABOUT]->(:Repo | :Package | :Advisory)

We parse real package-lock.json files using Node's own module-resolution rules, so the graph holds what is installed, not just what is declared. Then we add advisories from OSV.dev and maintainer usernames from the npm registry. The result is 17 repos, 11,179 package versions, 33,233 dependency edges, 357 advisories and 4,099 maintainers. It fits in about 19 MB.

Two modelling choices did most of the work:

  1. Every dependency edge stores its semver range. That's how we answer "would a lockfile refresh pull the hijacked version?", the question that mattered on September 8 and that lockfile scanners can't answer.
  2. Maintainers are nodes. "If this account is phished" becomes a traversal: person → packages → every version → every repo that reaches one.

The core query is short:

MATCH (:Package {name: $name})-[:HAS_VERSION]->(v:Version)
MATCH (r:Repo)
WITH r, v, shortestPath((r)-[:DEPENDS_ON*]->(v)) AS p
WHERE p IS NOT NULL
WITH r, v, p ORDER BY length(p)
WITH r, collect(v.version) AS versions, collect(p)[0] AS p
RETURN r.name, length(p), [n IN nodes(p) | coalesce(n.id, n.name)]

On a laptop, it answers for all 17 repos in about 30 ms. We also use FalkorDB's built-in algorithms as tools: algo.SPpaths to list every equally short chain between a repo and a package, and algo.pageRank to find the "next xz".

How the agent works

We set one rule early: the model never writes Cypher.

The agent picks from 13 fixed tools, served over MCP. Each tool runs a parameterised query we wrote and tested. Before any traversal runs, the tool checks that the package, repo, maintainer or advisory actually exists in the graph. Unknown names get suggestions back, never a guess.

Every result carries an explicit outcome: answered, not_in_graph, unknown_package or answered_from_memory. That's what keeps the agent honest. For the real Sept 2025 advisory, it says "not in the graph, not that you're safe" and then checks the ranges, instead of announcing an all-clear.

The model is Groq's gpt-oss-120b. The free tier is small (8,000 tokens a minute), so the model only reads the first rows of each tool result, plus a count. The UI still draws every path, because it gets the full result separately. The same 13 tools also work in Claude Code or Claude Desktop over MCP: the web agent is just one client.

The tracks we entered, and why it fits

Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data

This track asks for agents that use the graph to decide and act: multi-hop reasoning, graph algorithms as tools, tool selection through MCP, and explainable results. That's Hijack Radar's core:

  • Multi-hop reasoning: every answer is a traversal across up to several hops, from maintainer to package to version to repo.
  • Graph algorithms as tools: shortestPath, algo.SPpaths and algo.pageRank are tools the agent chooses.
  • MCP tool selection: 13 fixed tools, and the model picks which ones to call.
  • Action: it suggests an npm overrides fix and drafts an issue for the team that owns the repo.
  • Explainable: every result carries its dependency path, drawn beside the answer.

Track 02: Agent Memory and Coordination

This track asks for agents that remember across sessions and keep separate memory per user or tenant:

  • Memory as graph nodes: a triage decision such as "pin debug with overrides" becomes a dated Decision node linked to the package. Later answers about debug, or about advisories that touch it, come back with that decision attached: who decided and when.
  • Shared across agents: the memory lives in the graph, not in a chat window, so every MCP client (our web agent, Claude Code, Claude Desktop) sees the same decisions.
  • One graph per company: each tenant gets its own isolated graph on the same FalkorDB instance (supplychain and supplychain:orbit in our demo). The server pins each chat to its tenant, and the model never even sees the tenant argument. Ask about debug as our second demo company, Orbit, and you get Orbit's 5 repos, none of which declare debug and all of which install it. Orbit's decisions never appear for anyone else.

Things that bit us

  • Unbounded path enumeration. Our first algo.SPpaths call hung when the target wasn't reachable, because it tried to enumerate every path in the tree. Running shortestPath first and passing its length as maxLen brought it down to a few milliseconds.
  • An empty graph is an error, not an empty result. A fresh cloud instance made our health check fail and the host restart the app in a loop. Now health reports the problem instead of crashing.
  • Lockfiles are subtle. Nested node_modules, symlinked workspaces, npm aliases (string-width-cjs is really string-width) and optional platform packages all have to be handled before the graph tells the truth.
  • Prompts need to say what the UI needs. On the first real run, the model answered "who installs debug?" from memory instead of calling the tool, so the graph never appeared. One line in the prompt ("call tools for every question; the page draws evidence only from this turn") fixed it.

Try it

Reet24-del / supply-chain-blast-radius

Hijack Radar: an agent that traces phished npm maintainers and hijacked releases through a FalkorDB dependency graph (Graph Hacks 2026)

Hijack Radar

An npm maintainer gets phished and a release is hijacked. What did you just install, including what your lockfile says is safe? Hijack Radar is an agent that traces account takeovers and hijacked releases through a FalkorDB graph of your real, installed dependency trees, and shows the path behind every answer.

Radar view (/radar.html): the 17 repos as dots on a radar, with one ring per dependency hop. Pick an attack, such as a phished maintainer or the Sept 2025 debug@4.4.2 hijack, and the sweep lights up every exposed repo on the ring where the graph reaches it.

CVE scanners answer "which of my pinned versions is vulnerable?". Hijack Radar answers the questions they can't:

  • "If this maintainer's account is phished, what can the attacker publish into our repos?" Maintainers are nodes, so an account takeover is a traversal from a person to packages to every…
View on GitHub

The README has the graph model and every Cypher query the product depends on.

Run it locally. Hijack Radar runs on your own machine with an embedded FalkorDB engine, no Docker and no cloud account needed:

git clone https://github.com/Reet24-del/supply-chain-blast-radius && cd supply-chain-blast-radius
uv sync --extra lite
echo "FALKORDB_LITE_PATH=.falkordb/lite.db" >> .env
echo "GROQ_API_KEY=your-free-key" >> .env     # free at console.groq.com
uv run blast-ingest --reset                    # loads the 17 real lockfiles (~3 min the first time)
uv run blast-web                               # http://localhost:8000, plus /radar.html

Prefer Docker? docker compose up -d starts FalkorDB with its browser UI, and the same code also runs against FalkorDB Cloud.
